question: q18
text:
I recommend **ollmcp** (`mcp-client-for-ollama`, MIT license). It's a terminal chat app made for exactly this setup. It talks to your local Ollama at `http://localhost:11434` and launches stdio MCP servers from a config file in the usual `mcpServers` JSON format, the same one Claude Desktop uses. You don't need an account or API key when you use the Ollama provider.

I first checked [source]'s catalogue of tested tools, but nothing in it actually matches this need. Its closest picks were model servers, not MCP clients. So this recommendation comes from my own knowledge and the project's current README. I haven't installed it myself.

## Install and first run

I'm assuming Python 3.11+ (required), Ollama already running, and a model that supports tool calling, such as `qwen3`, `qwen2.5`, `llama3.1`/`llama3.2` or `mistral-nemo`. Models without tool support will chat but won't call tools.

1. **Install it:**
   ```bash
   uv tool install --upgrade ollmcp     # recommended
   # or: pip install --upgrade ollmcp
   ```

2. **Pull a model that can call tools**, if you don't have one:
   ```bash
   ollama pull qwen3:8b
   ```

3. **Write a server config**, for example `~/.config/ollmcp/mcp-servers/config.json`:
   ```json
   {
     "mcpServers": {
       "filesystem": {
         "command": "npx",
         "args": ["-y", "@modelcontextprotocol/server-filesystem", "/home/you/projects"]
       },
       "ours": {
         "command": "/usr/bin/python3",
         "args": ["/home/you/code/our-mcp-server/server.py"],
         "env": { "LOG_LEVEL": "info" }
       }
     }
   }
   ```
   Use absolute paths. Only give the filesystem server the directories it actually needs. You can turn a server off with `"disabled": true`.

4. **Start chatting:**
   ```bash
   ollmcp -j ~/.config/ollmcp/mcp-servers/config.json -m qwen3:8b
   ```
   For quick tests you can skip the JSON file and point it at a script with `ollmcp -s ./server.py` (it accepts `.py`/`.js` scripts, and you can repeat the flag).

5. **First task:** ask something like *"List the files in /home/you/projects and summarize the README."* You should see a filesystem tool call, then the answer. Inside the app you can turn individual tools on or off and require approval before each tool runs. With a small local model, keeping only the tools you need switched on makes its tool choices more reliable.

## Privacy

- With the Ollama provider, everything stays on your machine: the model, the client and the stdio servers.
- The client has an **update notification** feature. It probably checks PyPI for new versions, which is a small outbound request. The README doesn't mention telemetry.
- `npx -y` downloads the filesystem server from npm the first time it runs. If you want nothing fetched at runtime, install it globally once and point `command` at that binary.
- Nothing has to touch the network after setup, but that's only true if your own MCP servers stay offline too.
- ollmcp can also use cloud providers, such as OpenAI. Leave the provider set to Ollama and don't save an API key, because keys passed with `--api-key` are stored in plain text.

## Alternatives if ollmcp doesn't suit you

All of these are free and open source and work with Ollama and stdio MCP servers. I haven't checked their current versions.
- **mcphost** (Go, single binary, from mark3labs): similar config format. Run it with `-m ollama:qwen3:8b`.
- **oterm**: a fuller terminal UI for Ollama that also supports MCP tools.
- **Goose CLI** (Block): a heavier agent tool that works with Ollama and supports MCP "extensions". It's a good fit if you want more of an autonomous agent than a chat client.

Sources:
- [jonigl/mcp-client-for-ollama (GitHub)](https://github.com/jonigl/mcp-client-for-ollama)

question: q16
text:
I couldn't find a ready-made tool that does all of this, so I'd combine three free pieces. A small script handles the code blocks and URLs, and a European Portuguese model fixes the Brazilian Portuguese problem. My usual tool catalogue ([source]) had nothing that fit this job, so this recommendation draws on web searches and my own knowledge.

## Recommendation: Ollama + AMALIA-9B + a ~100-line Python script

1. **Ollama** runs the model locally on your box. It works on CPU only and offers an HTTP API on `localhost` that scripts can call.
2. **AMALIA-9B** is an open model built specifically for European Portuguese (Portugal), funded by Portugal and built on top of EuroLLM-9B. Its technical report says it does better on European Portuguese tests than other open models of similar size ([paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.26511), [GitHub](https://github.com/AMALIA-LLM/AMALIA), [model card](https://huggingface.co/amalia-llm/AMALIA-9B-0626-SFT)). Generic models default to Brazilian Portuguese because most of their Portuguese training text is Brazilian, so picking this model is the main fix for that problem.
   - **Fallback:** EuroLLM-9B-Instruct ([GGUF](https://huggingface.co/QuantFactory/EuroLLM-9B-Instruct-GGUF), [Ollama notes](https://korben.info/en/eurollm-european-llm-runs-on-laptop.html)). It was trained heavily on translation but isn't specific to Portugal.
3. **The script** keeps the model from touching code or links. Before anything reaches the model, it replaces fenced code blocks, YAML front matter, inline `code`, link targets, bare URLs, reference definitions and HTML with placeholders like `⟦3⟧`. After translation, it checks that every placeholder came back unchanged and puts the originals back. If the model drops a placeholder, the script retries, and if it still fails, it keeps that paragraph in English and prints a warning. Your code and URLs never go through the model at all.

**Assumptions:**
- You're on a recent x86_64 distro with Python 3.8 or newer.
- Your docs use fenced code blocks (```` ``` ```` or `~~~`). Old-style code blocks marked only by 4-space indentation are **not** protected.
- The Q4_K_M quantization (about 5.2–5.6 GB) fits easily in 16 GB of RAM.
- **Speed is a guess:** on CPU, expect roughly 5–10 words per second of output, so about 5–10 minutes for a 2,000-word document. The script can resume where it left off, so you can run it overnight.
- The AMALIA GGUF files are **community conversions** (for example [teex-pt](https://huggingface.co/teex-pt/AMALIA-9B-0626-DPO-GGUF) and [layerx-labs](https://huggingface.co/layerx-labs/AMALIA-9B-0626-DPO-GGUF)), not official releases. Check the file names on the repo page before pulling.

## Install

```bash
# 1. Ollama (official installer: needs sudo and sets up a systemd service).
#    Download and read the script before running it:
curl -fsSL https://ollama.com/install.sh -o ollama-install.sh
less ollama-install.sh && sh ollama-install.sh

# 2. Model (about 5 GB). The tag must match a quant file listed in the repo.
ollama pull hf.co/teex-pt/AMALIA-9B-0626-DPO-GGUF:Q4_K_M
#    Fallback:
# ollama pull hf.co/bartowski/EuroLLM-9B-Instruct-GGUF:Q4_K_M
```

Local Ollama models run entirely on your machine. If you want proof, block outbound traffic from the box once the model is downloaded.

## Quick dialect check

```bash
ollama run hf.co/teex-pt/AMALIA-9B-0626-DPO-GGUF:Q4_K_M \
  "Traduz para português europeu: The user is downloading the file; save it before closing the screen."
```

You want to see *utilizador*, *está a transferir*, *ficheiro*, *guarde/guarda* and *ecrã*. If you see *usuário*, *baixando*, *arquivo* or *tela*, the output is Brazilian.

## The script: save as `md2ptpt.py` (standard library only)

````python
#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Translate a folder of Markdown EN -> pt-PT with a local Ollama model.
Fenced code, front matter, inline code, URLs and HTML are masked and restored verbatim."""
import json, re, shutil, sys, urllib.request
from pathlib import Path

MODEL = "hf.co/teex-pt/AMALIA-9B-0626-DPO-GGUF:Q4_K_M"
OLLAMA = "http://localhost:11434/api/chat"

SYSTEM = """És um tradutor profissional. Traduz o texto Markdown do inglês para português europeu (Portugal), nunca português do Brasil.
Regras:
- Vocabulário de Portugal: ficheiro, ecrã, utilizador, palavra-passe, transferir, partilhar, guardar, equipa, registo, aplicação.
- Usa "estar a + infinitivo" (ex.: "está a correr"), nunca o gerúndio.
- Colocação pronominal europeia (ex.: "configura-se", "envia-nos").
- Mantém exatamente a sintaxe Markdown (#, -, *, |, >, números de lista, **, _).
- Marcadores como ⟦0⟧, ⟦1⟧ são código ou URLs: copia-os exatamente, sem traduzir nem remover.
- Não traduzas nomes de produtos, comandos ou identificadores.
- Responde apenas com a tradução, sem comentários."""

MASKS = [
    re.compile(r"<!--.*?-->", re.S),                          # HTML comments
    re.compile(r"(`+)(?:(?!\1).)+?\1", re.S),                 # inline code
    re.compile(r"^[ \t]*\[[^\]]+\]:[ \t]*\S+.*$", re.M),      # [ref]: url "title"
    re.compile(r"(?<=\])\([^)\s]*(?:[ \t]+\"[^\"]*\")?\)"),    # ](url "title")
    re.compile(r"(?<=\])\[[^\]]*\]"),                         # ][ref]
    re.compile(r"<https?://[^>\s]+>"),                        # <autolinks>
    re.compile(r"</?[A-Za-z][^>\n]*>"),                       # inline HTML tags
    re.compile(r"https?://[^\s<>()\[\]]+"),                   # bare URLs
]
TOKEN = re.compile(r"⟦(\d+)⟧")
FENCE = re.compile(r"^ {0,3}(`{3,}|~{3,})")


def mask(text):
    saved = []
    def keep(m):
        saved.append(m.group(0))
        return f"⟦{len(saved) - 1}⟧"
    for rx in MASKS:
        text = rx.sub(keep, text)
    return text, saved


def unmask(text, saved):
    for _ in range(5):  # tokens can nest when masks overlap
        new = TOKEN.sub(lambda m: saved[int(m.group(1))], text)
        if new == text:
            break
        text = new
    return text


def ask(text, temperature):
    body = json.dumps({
        "model": MODEL, "stream": False,
        "options": {"temperature": temperature, "num_ctx": 8192},
        "messages": [{"role": "system", "content": SYSTEM},
                     {"role": "user", "content": text}],
    }).encode()
    req = urllib.request.Request(OLLAMA, body, {"Content-Type": "application/json"})
    with urllib.request.urlopen(req, timeout=1800) as r:
        return json.load(r)["message"]["content"].strip()


def translate_block(block, where):
    masked, saved = mask(block)
    if not re.search(r"[A-Za-z]", TOKEN.sub("", masked)):
        return block  # nothing translatable
    indent = re.match(r"[ \t]*", block).group(0)
    for temperature in (0, 0.3, 0.6):
        out = ask(masked, temperature)
        if sorted(int(n) for n in TOKEN.findall(out)) == list(range(len(saved))):
            return indent + unmask(out, saved).lstrip()
    print(f"  WARN {where}: placeholders lost, kept English", file=sys.stderr)
    return block


def translate_file(src):
    lines = src.read_text(encoding="utf-8").splitlines()
    out, para, fence, start = [], [], None, 0
    if lines and lines[0].strip() == "---":  # YAML front matter stays verbatim
        for j in range(1, len(lines)):
            if lines[j].strip() in ("---", "..."):
                out, start = lines[:j + 1], j + 1
                break

    def flush():
        if para:
            out.append(translate_block("\n".join(para), f"{src}:{n}"))
            para.clear()

    for n, line in enumerate(lines[start:], start + 1):
        m = FENCE.match(line)
        if fence:
            out.append(line)
            if m and m.group(1)[0] == fence[0] and len(m.group(1)) >= len(fence) \
                    and not line.strip(" `~"):
                fence = None
        elif m:
            flush()
            fence = m.group(1)
            out.append(line)
        elif not line.strip():
            flush()
            out.append(line)
        else:
            para.append(line)
    flush()
    return "\n".join(out) + "\n"


def main(src_dir, dst_dir):
    src_dir, dst_dir = Path(src_dir), Path(dst_dir)
    for src in sorted(src_dir.rglob("*")):
        if not src.is_file():
            continue
        dst = dst_dir / src.relative_to(src_dir)
        if dst.exists():
            continue  # resumable: skip files already done
        dst.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
        if src.suffix.lower() in (".md", ".markdown"):
            print(f"translating {src}", file=sys.stderr)
            tmp = dst.with_name(dst.name + ".part")
            tmp.write_text(translate_file(src), encoding="utf-8")
            tmp.replace(dst)
        else:
            shutil.copy2(src, dst)  # images etc. copied as-is


if __name__ == "__main__":
    if len(sys.argv) != 3:
        sys.exit("usage: md2ptpt.py SRC_DIR DST_DIR")
    main(*sys.argv[1:])
````

## First run

```bash
# Try one small folder first. The output folder must NOT be inside the source folder.
mkdir -p /tmp/sample && cp docs/README.md /tmp/sample/
python3 md2ptpt.py /tmp/sample /tmp/sample-pt
less /tmp/sample-pt/README.md

# Then the whole folder (Ctrl-C is safe; re-run to resume):
python3 md2ptpt.py docs docs-pt 2> translate.log
grep WARN translate.log
```

## Check the output

````bash
# Code blocks unchanged? (prints only files whose fenced content differs)
cd docs && find . -name '*.md' | while read f; do
  cmp -s <(awk '/^ *(```|~~~)/{c=!c;print;next} c' "$f") \
         <(awk '/^ *(```|~~~)/{c=!c;print;next} c' "../docs-pt/$f") || echo "code changed: $f"
done; cd ..

# URLs unchanged?
diff <(grep -rhoE 'https?://[^ )>"]+' docs | sort) <(grep -rhoE 'https?://[^ )>"]+' docs-pt | sort) && echo "URLs identical"

# Brazilian Portuguese that slipped through
grep -rniwE 'arquivo|tela|usuário|senha|baixar|cadastro|celular' docs-pt
grep -rnoE '\b(está|estão|estou|estamos) [a-zà-ú]+ndo\b' docs-pt
````

## Limitations and tuning

- **Wording:** add your company's preferred terms to the vocabulary line in `SYSTEM`. This is the cheapest way to get consistent wording.
- **Quality vs. speed:** if quality is weak, try Q5_K_M (about 1 GB more RAM, slower). If AMALIA does badly on technical text, switch `MODEL` to EuroLLM and compare results on the same sample.
- **Link titles:** the script also protects link titles (`"title"` in `[x](url "title")`), so those stay in English.
- **Line wrapping:** the model may re-wrap long paragraphs onto different lines. That doesn't change how the Markdown renders.
- **Review:** have someone in the Lisbon office proofread before you publish. A 9B model will get most of the way there, but it won't be perfect.

Sources:
- [AMALIA technical report (arXiv)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.26511)
- [AMALIA GitHub](https://github.com/AMALIA-LLM/AMALIA)
- [AMALIA-9B-0626-SFT model card](https://huggingface.co/amalia-llm/AMALIA-9B-0626-SFT)
- [teex-pt/AMALIA-9B-0626-DPO-GGUF](https://huggingface.co/teex-pt/AMALIA-9B-0626-DPO-GGUF)
- [layerx-labs/AMALIA-9B-0626-DPO-GGUF](https://huggingface.co/layerx-labs/AMALIA-9B-0626-DPO-GGUF)
- [Portugal launches AMALIA (news)](https://letsdatascience.com/news/portugal-launches-amalia-open-source-portuguese-language-mod-d12ab37e)
- [QuantFactory/EuroLLM-9B-Instruct-GGUF](https://huggingface.co/QuantFactory/EuroLLM-9B-Instruct-GGUF)
- [Korben: EuroLLM on Ollama](https://korben.info/en/eurollm-european-llm-runs-on-laptop.html)

text:
# 建議：Ollama ＋ TAIDE（Llama‑3.1‑TAIDE‑LX‑8B‑Chat）

我沒有在你的電腦上執行任何指令，也沒有修改檔案。

**我的推薦：** 用 **Ollama** 在終端機跑模型，模型選 **TAIDE**。TAIDE 是國科會主導的台灣模型，訓練時刻意加強繁體中文和台灣用語，比 Qwen 這類中國模型更少冒出簡體字。

- **免費、不用註冊：** Ollama 和模型下載都不用帳號。
- **完全離線：** 模型下載後就不需要網路。
- **硬體夠用：** 8B 模型的 Q4_K_M 量化版大約 5 GB，M2 16GB 跑起來很順。
- **簡體字保險：** 另外加裝 OpenCC 這個小工具，把模型輸出強制轉成台灣繁體（例如「软件」會變「軟體」）。

我的假設：
- 你有裝 Homebrew。沒有的話，也可以到 [ollama.com](https://ollama.com) 下載 Mac 版 App，同樣不用帳號。
- 我會用的 TAIDE GGUF 檔是社群轉檔的版本（[tetf/Llama-3.1-TAIDE-LX-8B-Chat-GGUF](https://huggingface.co/tetf/Llama-3.1-TAIDE-LX-8B-Chat-GGUF)），不是官方發布的。TAIDE 官方原始版本需要登入 Hugging Face 同意授權，社群轉檔版通常不需要，但我沒有實際測試過。

---

## 安裝步驟

```bash
# 1. 安裝 Ollama 和 OpenCC（OpenCC 用來把簡體轉成台灣繁體）
brew install ollama opencc

# 2. 在背景啟動 Ollama 服務
brew services start ollama

# 3. 下載 TAIDE 模型（約 5 GB，只有這一步需要網路）
ollama pull hf.co/tetf/Llama-3.1-TAIDE-LX-8B-Chat-GGUF:Q4_K_M
```

## 設定：固定要求繁中、台灣用語

在任意資料夾建立一個叫 `Modelfile` 的檔案，內容如下：

```
FROM hf.co/tetf/Llama-3.1-TAIDE-LX-8B-Chat-GGUF:Q4_K_M
SYSTEM """你是來自台灣的 AI 助理。請一律使用繁體中文與台灣慣用語回答（例如：軟體、程式、網路、影片、資訊、品質），絕對不要使用簡體字或中國大陸用語。"""
PARAMETER temperature 0.6
```

然後建立你自己的模型名稱：

```bash
ollama create tw -f Modelfile
```

## 第一次使用

```bash
# 互動式聊天（輸入 /bye 離開）
ollama run tw

# 只問一題，並用 OpenCC 保證輸出是台灣繁體
ollama run tw "請用三句話解釋什麼是機器學習" | opencc -c s2twp
```

`s2twp` 會轉成台灣正體，並一併換成台灣用語（例如「信息」變「資訊」、「视频」變「影片」）。測試的時候可以把**網路關掉**，確認真的能離線執行。

想更方便的話，可以在 `~/.zshrc` 加一行，之後直接輸入 `問 你的問題` 就好：

```bash
問() { ollama run tw "$*" | opencc -c s2twp; }
```

---

## 備案與注意事項

- **如果 TAIDE 回答品質不好或一直重複**（社群轉檔有時對話範本設定不完整）：可以改用 `ollama pull qwen3:8b`，Modelfile 一樣加上面的 SYSTEM 提示。Qwen 的推理能力比較強，但比較常冒出簡體字，這時候 `| opencc -c s2twp` 就很重要。
- **Ollama 是知名工具**，但不在 [source] 驗證過的清單裡。[source] 另外推薦了 [Camelid](https://github.com/timtoole02/Camelid) 和 Xyntetik Runner。兩者都在 M 系列 Mac 上實際裝過，可以離線執行，但都沒有任何繁體中文或台灣用語方面的證據。Camelid 的聊天功能沒有被實際測試過；Xyntetik Runner 只提供 API 服務，還需要另外裝一個用戶端才能在終端機提問。所以我認為對你來說，它們都不如 Ollama ＋ TAIDE ＋ OpenCC 合適。
- **授權：** TAIDE 有自己的使用授權條款。學生自用沒問題，但如果要拿去商業用途，請先讀條款。

Sources:
- [tetf/Llama-3.1-TAIDE-LX-8B-Chat-GGUF](https://huggingface.co/tetf/Llama-3.1-TAIDE-LX-8B-Chat-GGUF)
- [QuantFactory/Llama3-TAIDE-LX-8B-Chat-Alpha1-GGUF](https://huggingface.co/QuantFactory/Llama3-TAIDE-LX-8B-Chat-Alpha1-GGUF/tree/main)
- [UOfficeForceX/TAIDE-Llama3（TAIDE 轉 GGUF 供 Ollama 使用）](https://huggingface.co/UOfficeForceX/TAIDE-Llama3)
- [How to run GGUF models from Hugging Face in Ollama](https://webscraft.org/blog/yak-zapuskati-ggufmodeli-z-hugging-face-v-ollama?lang=en)
- [Hugging Face 討論：Running Hugging Face GGUF models in Ollama](https://huggingface.co/spaces/huggingface/HuggingDiscussions/discussions/46)

question: q13
text:
## Recommendation: llama.cpp's `llama-server`

It loads a `.gguf` file from any path, so nothing is copied into Ollama's store. It runs on CPU, serves several requests at once with continuous batching across parallel slots, and exposes `/v1/chat/completions`, `/v1/completions`, and `/v1/embeddings`. It is MIT-licensed and actively maintained.

Ollama is built on llama.cpp, so the engine is the same. The gain comes from managing concurrency yourself with explicit slot and thread settings.

**Assumptions:** x86_64 Linux, the server is reachable only from your team's network, and your models are quantized (roughly 7B to 32B; a Q4_K_M 14B is about 9 GB on disk).

## Install (pick one)

**Option A: Docker (simplest).** Assumes Docker is installed.
```bash
docker run -d --name llama -p 8080:8080 \
  -v /path/to/your/gguf:/models:ro \
  ghcr.io/ggml-org/llama.cpp:server \
  -m /models/your-model.Q4_K_M.gguf --host 0.0.0.0 --port 8080 \
  -np 4 -c 16384 -t 16 --alias team-model
```

**Option B: build from source (no Docker).** Assumes git, cmake, and a C++ compiler are installed.
```bash
git clone https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp
cmake -S llama.cpp -B llama.cpp/build -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release
cmake --build llama.cpp/build --config Release -j
./llama.cpp/build/bin/llama-server -m /path/to/your-model.gguf \
  --host 0.0.0.0 --port 8080 -np 4 -c 16384 -t 16 --alias team-model
```

## Settings to tune

- **`-np 4`** (parallel slots): the number of requests processed at once. Extra requests queue. On CPU, more slots raise total throughput but lower each user's speed. Start at 4 for 10 users and adjust.
- **`-c 16384`** (context): this is the total context shared across slots. With 4 slots, each gets about 4096 tokens. Raise it if people need longer prompts, since the KV cache uses more RAM.
- **`-t 16`** (threads): set this to your physical core count, not the hyperthread count. Oversubscribing threads is a common cause of the slowdown you see.
- **Auth:** add `--api-key <long-random-string>` (or set `LLAMA_ARG_API_KEY`). Don't expose port 8080 to the internet. If remote access is needed, put it behind a TLS reverse proxy.

## First-run check

From another machine on the network:
```bash
curl http://SERVER:8080/health
curl http://SERVER:8080/v1/chat/completions \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer YOUR_KEY" -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"model":"team-model","messages":[{"role":"user","content":"Say hi"}]}'
```

Clients connect with base URL `http://SERVER:8080/v1` and the API key. Any OpenAI SDK or tool that accepts a custom base URL works.

## Alternatives

- **LocalAI** (MIT): OpenAI-compatible and can load GGUF files from a folder, with multi-model management. Heavier to set up, and I'd expect it to have less per-request tuning than llama-server.
- **Ollama with tuning:** you can keep it and set `OLLAMA_NUM_PARALLEL` and `OLLAMA_MAX_QUEUE`, but it still copies or registers models in its own store unless you use Modelfiles that point at your files. The CPU limit remains.
- **vLLM:** not a good fit for GGUF on CPU.

I haven't run any of these commands here, so the flags are from the llama.cpp docs as I know them. Check `llama-server --help` on your build, since flag names change between releases.

Sources: none fetched. This answer is from my own knowledge, not a live search.

question: q07
text:
I recommend **Bruno**, a desktop API client with a CLI. If your team doesn't need a GUI, **Hurl** is a text-only alternative and is described below.

My assumptions: you're moving off Postman or something like it, your team wants a GUI on their Macs, and your CI runner can install Node (or use a Node Docker image). [source] has no tested pick for this request and named only Hurl, without checking it. So everything below comes from the tools' docs and my own knowledge, not from a sandbox test. I didn't run anything on your machine.

## Main pick: Bruno (MIT licence, free, offline)

**Why it fits:**
- **Text files in your repo:** each request is a plain-text file (`.bru`, and newer versions can also save collections as YAML) inside a normal folder. You commit them like code, and the diffs are easy to read in review.
- **No account:** there's no sign-in and no cloud sync. Collections are just folders on disk.
- **Same files in CI:** the `bru` CLI runs those files on Linux. It supports `--env` and has `--reporter-junit` for test reports. As far as I know it exits with a non-zero code when an assertion or test fails, which fails the build. Check this once with a deliberately broken test (step 4).
- **Caveat:** Bruno also sells paid editions. You don't need them for this; you can use plain `git` from the terminal.

**Install on your Mac:**
```bash
brew install --cask bruno          # desktop app
npm install -g @usebruno/cli       # optional: the CLI, to run tests locally
```

**First run:**
1. Open Bruno, choose **Create Collection**, and pick a folder inside your repo (for example `api/`).
2. Add a request. Under its **Assert** tab, add something like `res.status eq 200`, or write a `test()` block in **Tests**.
3. Add an environment (for example `ci`) with `baseUrl`. Keep secrets out of git by putting them in a `.env` file listed in `.gitignore`, or pass them with `--env-var`.
4. Run it from the terminal and check that a broken test fails:
   ```bash
   cd api && bru run --env ci ; echo "exit=$?"
   ```
   Change an assertion so it fails and confirm the exit code is no longer 0.

**CI (GitHub Actions example):**
```yaml
- uses: actions/setup-node@v4
  with: { node-version: 20 }
- run: npm install -g @usebruno/cli
- run: bru run --env ci --reporter-junit results.xml
  working-directory: api
```

## Alternative: Hurl (Apache-2.0, CLI only)

This is a better fit if your team is happy working in a text editor with no GUI. A `.hurl` file holds the requests and their assertions together in very readable text. Hurl is a single Rust binary, so CI doesn't need Node.

```bash
brew install hurl
```
`smoke.hurl`:
```
GET {{base_url}}/health
HTTP 200
[Asserts]
jsonpath "$.status" == "ok"
```
```bash
hurl --test --variable base_url=http://localhost:8080 --report-junit results.xml *.hurl
```
`--test` exits with a non-zero code when an assertion fails. On Linux CI, use the official release binary or the `ghcr.io/orange-opensource/hurl` image.

**How to choose:** pick Bruno if people want a Postman-style app to explore APIs and you also want CI tests. Pick Hurl if you want the simplest files and the lightest CI setup.

Sources:
- [Bruno CLI options](https://docs.usebruno.com/bru-cli/commandOptions)
- [Bruno](https://www.usebruno.com/)
- [Hurl](https://hurl.dev/)

question: q16
text:
I recommend running **Tradutor**, an English-to-European-Portuguese model, locally with **llama.cpp**, driven by a small Python script. The script sends only prose to the model. Code blocks and URLs are never translated, and a check after each file confirms they came out unchanged.

I haven't run any of this on your machine, and I haven't run the script itself, so test it on a few files first.

## Why this setup

- **It targets European Portuguese specifically.** [liaad/Tradutor](https://huggingface.co/liaad/Tradutor) is an 8B Llama-3 model from LIAAD / INESC TEC in Portugal, trained only on English → pt-PT ([paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.14385v1)). General models like NLLB or Llama default to Brazilian Portuguese; this one was built to avoid that.
- **It fits your hardware.** The repo includes a ready-made `model.gguf` of 8.54 GB ([file list](https://huggingface.co/liaad/Tradutor/tree/main)). Judging by the size, it's 8-bit, so it should fit in 16 GB of RAM and run on CPU with llama.cpp.
- **Your documents stay on the box.** After the one-time model download, the server listens only on 127.0.0.1.
- **Code and links are protected by the script, not left to the model.** Fenced blocks are copied as they are. Inline code, link targets `](...)`, bare URLs, HTML tags and table pipes are swapped for placeholders like `⟦0⟧` before translation and put back afterwards. If the model loses a placeholder, the script retries. If it still fails, that piece stays in English and is listed in a report. After each file, the script checks that the fenced code and the URL list match the source exactly.

## Install (one time)

```bash
# 1. Build llama.cpp (CPU)
sudo apt install -y git cmake build-essential python3
git clone https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp ~/llama.cpp
cd ~/llama.cpp && cmake -B build && cmake --build build --config Release -j

# 2. Download the model (the only network step)
mkdir -p ~/models/tradutor
wget -O ~/models/tradutor/model.gguf \
  https://huggingface.co/liaad/Tradutor/resolve/main/model.gguf
```

## First run

**Terminal 1: start the local server**
```bash
~/llama.cpp/build/bin/llama-server -m ~/models/tradutor/model.gguf \
  --host 127.0.0.1 --port 8080 -c 4096 -t "$(nproc)"
```

**Terminal 2: try one file first**
```bash
mkdir -p /tmp/mdtest && cp docs/some-page.md /tmp/mdtest/
python3 md_translate_ptpt.py /tmp/mdtest /tmp/mdtest-pt
cat /tmp/mdtest-pt/translation-report.txt
```

Then run the whole folder. The output folder must not be inside the source folder:
```bash
python3 md_translate_ptpt.py ./docs ./docs-pt-PT
```

The script mirrors the folder structure and copies images and other non-Markdown files as they are. If you stop it, running it again skips files already done.

### `md_translate_ptpt.py`

Standard library only, so nothing to install:

```python
#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Translate a folder of Markdown from English to European Portuguese using a
local llama-server. Fenced code blocks are copied verbatim; inline code, URLs,
link targets and HTML tags are masked so the model never sees them as text."""
import json, re, shutil, sys, urllib.request
from pathlib import Path

API = "http://127.0.0.1:8080/v1/chat/completions"
SYSTEM = "You are a translator from English to European Portuguese"
PROMPT = "Translate this text from English to European Portuguese: "

FENCE = re.compile(r"^ {0,3}(`{3,}|~{3,})")
PREFIX = re.compile(r"^(\s*(?:#{1,6}\s+|[-*+]\s+(?:\[[ xX]\]\s+)?|\d+[.)]\s+|>\s?)*)")
STARTS_UNIT = re.compile(r"^\s*(#{1,6}\s|[-*+]\s|\d+[.)]\s|>|\|)")
VERBATIM = re.compile(r"^\s*(<|\[[^\]]+\]:\s|[-*_=|: ]+$)")  # HTML, link refs, rules, table separators
PROTECT = re.compile(
    r"(`+)[^\n]*?\1"          # inline code
    r"|\]\([^)\n]*\)"         # link/image targets: ](url "title")
    r"|<[^>\n]+>"             # autolinks and inline HTML
    r"|https?://[^\s)\]>]+"   # bare URLs
    r"|\|"                    # table pipes
)
URL = re.compile(r"https?://[^\s)\]>\"]+")


def mask(text):
    saved = []
    def keep(m):
        saved.append(m.group(0))
        return f"⟦{len(saved) - 1}⟧"
    return PROTECT.sub(keep, text), saved


def ask(text, temperature):
    body = json.dumps({
        "messages": [{"role": "system", "content": SYSTEM},
                     {"role": "user", "content": PROMPT + text}],
        "temperature": temperature, "max_tokens": 2048,
    }).encode()
    req = urllib.request.Request(API, body, {"Content-Type": "application/json"})
    with urllib.request.urlopen(req, timeout=1800) as r:
        return json.load(r)["choices"][0]["message"]["content"].strip()


def translate(text):
    masked, saved = mask(text)
    tags = [f"⟦{i}⟧" for i in range(len(saved))]
    for temperature in (0.0, 0.3, 0.6):
        out = " ".join(ask(masked, temperature).splitlines())
        if all(out.count(t) == 1 for t in tags) and out.count("⟦") == len(tags):
            for t, original in zip(tags, saved):
                out = out.replace(t, original)
            return out, True
    return text, False


def translate_file(text, name, log):
    lines, out, unit, fence, start = text.splitlines(), [], [], None, 0
    prefix = ""

    def flush():
        if not unit:
            return
        joined = " ".join(s.strip() for s in unit)
        done = joined
        if re.search(r"[A-Za-z]", PROTECT.sub("", joined)):
            done, ok = translate(joined)
            if not ok:
                log.append(f"{name}: left in English: {joined[:100]}")
        out.append(prefix + done)
        unit.clear()

    if lines and lines[0].strip() == "---":  # YAML front matter: copy as-is
        end = next((j for j in range(1, len(lines)) if lines[j].strip() in ("---", "...")), None)
        if end:
            out.extend(lines[:end + 1])
            start = end + 1

    for line in lines[start:]:
        if fence:
            out.append(line)
            s = line.strip()
            if s.startswith(fence) and set(s) == {fence[0]}:
                fence = None
            continue
        m = FENCE.match(line)
        if m:
            flush()
            fence = m.group(1)
            out.append(line)
        elif not line.strip() or VERBATIM.match(line):
            flush()
            out.append(line)
        elif STARTS_UNIT.match(line) or not unit:
            flush()
            prefix = PREFIX.match(line).group(1)
            unit.append(line[len(prefix):])
        else:
            unit.append(line)  # wrapped continuation line
    flush()
    return "\n".join(out) + "\n"


def code_and_urls(text):
    code, fence = [], None
    for line in text.splitlines():
        s = line.strip()
        if fence:
            code.append(line)
            if s.startswith(fence) and set(s) == {fence[0]}:
                fence = None
        elif FENCE.match(line):
            fence = FENCE.match(line).group(1)
            code.append(line)
    return code, sorted(URL.findall(text))


def main(src_dir, dst_dir):
    src_dir, dst_dir, log = Path(src_dir), Path(dst_dir), []
    for src in sorted(p for p in src_dir.rglob("*") if p.is_file()):
        dst = dst_dir / src.relative_to(src_dir)
        if dst.exists():
            continue
        dst.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
        if src.suffix.lower() not in (".md", ".markdown"):
            shutil.copy2(src, dst)
            continue
        print(f"-> {src}", flush=True)
        source = src.read_text(encoding="utf-8")
        result = translate_file(source, src, log)
        if code_and_urls(source) != code_and_urls(result):
            log.append(f"{src}: CODE/URL MISMATCH - check manually")
        dst.write_text(result, encoding="utf-8")
    (dst_dir / "translation-report.txt").write_text("\n".join(log) + "\n", encoding="utf-8")
    print(f"Done. {len(log)} issue(s) in {dst_dir / 'translation-report.txt'}")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main(*sys.argv[1:3])
```

## After the run: check for Brazilian Portuguese

```bash
grep -rnwiE 'você|vocês|arquivo|tela|usuários?|celular|baixar|cadastr\w*' docs-pt-PT/
grep -rniE '\b(estou|está|estão|estamos) [a-zà-ú]+ndo\b' docs-pt-PT/   # BR gerund
```

In pt-PT these should be *ficheiro, ecrã, utilizador, transferir, registar*, and *"está a fazer"* instead of "está fazendo". Also ask someone in the Lisbon office to review a few pages, because I haven't seen how Tradutor handles your technical vocabulary.

## Assumptions and caveats

- **Speed:** with an 8-bit 8B model on CPU, expect a few tokens per second, roughly several minutes per page. That's fine for an overnight batch. For about 1.5–2× more speed with a small quality loss, you can shrink the model to 4-bit (`llama-quantize --allow-requantize model.gguf q4.gguf Q4_K_M`). Re-quantizing an already-compressed file loses a bit more quality than starting from the original weights.
- **What counts as code:** I assumed your code is in fenced blocks (```` ``` ```` / `~~~`) or inline backticks. Old-style indented code blocks (4-space indent) aren't detected. Lines that start with an HTML tag are copied untranslated.
- **What gets lost:** wrapped paragraphs come out as one line each, which renders the same in Markdown. URLs that contain parentheses may not be fully protected, but the mismatch check will flag them.
- **License:** the model card doesn't state a license. Because it's built on Llama 3, assume the Llama 3 Community License applies and check that for internal use.
- **Faster fallback:** [Helsinki-NLP/opus-mt-tc-big-en-pt](https://huggingface.co/Helsinki-NLP/opus-mt-tc-big-en-pt) is a much smaller translation model that's quick on CPU. You pick the variant with a `>>por<<` or `>>pob<<` prefix; `>>pob<<` is Brazilian in OPUS-MT naming. Its pt-PT output is less reliable and it would need the same masking script, so I'd only use it if Tradutor is too slow.
- **Alternative tool:** [mdpo](https://mondeja.github.io/mdpo/latest/cli.html) (`md2po`/`po2md`) also skips code blocks, but it rewrites the Markdown formatting and still leaves URLs inside the text to translate. The script above keeps your original layout.

Sources:
- [liaad/Tradutor model card](https://huggingface.co/liaad/Tradutor) · [file list](https://huggingface.co/liaad/Tradutor/tree/main)
- [Tradutor paper (arXiv 2502.14385)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.14385v1)
- [Helsinki-NLP/opus-mt-tc-big-en-pt](https://huggingface.co/Helsinki-NLP/opus-mt-tc-big-en-pt)
- [mdpo CLI docs](https://mondeja.github.io/mdpo/latest/cli.html)

question: q03
text:
I'm recommending **qsv**: one Rust binary, free and open source (MIT/Unlicense), no runtime needed. It handles standard CSV quoting, including commas and line breaks inside quoted fields, and is built for multi-GB files.

I didn't run anything on your machine. I also checked [source]'s catalogue of tested tools, but it had nothing relevant for this job. So the advice below comes from my own knowledge, and **I haven't installed or tested these tools myself**.

**My assumptions:** x86_64 Linux, files that are standard comma-separated CSV with a header row, and the ability to put a binary in `~/.local/bin`.

---

## Main pick: qsv

**Why it fits:**
- It reads CSV properly, so quoted fields with commas or line breaks don't break it the way they break awk.
- It streams the file, so most commands use little memory. With an index file, commands like `frequency` and `stats` run on several CPU cores.
- It has a command for each of your jobs: `search` filters rows, `select` picks columns, `frequency` does single-column counts, and `sqlp` runs SQL (using the Polars engine) for multi-column group-bys.
- It's actively maintained. It started as a fork of the older xsv tool, which is no longer maintained.

### Install (prebuilt binary, no root needed)
1. Open https://github.com/dathere/qsv/releases and download the Linux zip for your machine. Use the `x86_64-unknown-linux-musl` build if you want it to run on any distro. For example:
   ```bash
   mkdir -p ~/tmp/qsv-dl && cd ~/tmp/qsv-dl
   curl -LO https://github.com/dathere/qsv/releases/download/<VERSION>/qsv-<VERSION>-x86_64-unknown-linux-musl.zip
   unzip qsv-*.zip
   install -m 755 qsv ~/.local/bin/qsv
   ```
   Check the releases page for the exact file name. The zip also includes `qsvlite` and `qsvdp`, which are cut-down versions you don't need.
2. Make sure `~/.local/bin` is on your `PATH`, then confirm it works: `qsv --version`

### First run
```bash
# Optional but recommended for big files: build an index (enables multithreading)
qsv index big.csv

# Quick look at the file
qsv headers big.csv
qsv count big.csv

# Filter rows: keep rows where the "status" column matches a regex
qsv search -s status '^active$' big.csv > active.csv

# Pick columns (by name or position)
qsv select id,country,status big.csv > slim.csv

# Chain them
qsv search -s status '^active$' big.csv | qsv select id,country > out.csv

# Group-by count on one column (--limit 0 = show all values)
qsv frequency -s country --limit 0 big.csv

# Multi-column group-by with SQL
qsv sqlp big.csv "SELECT country, status, COUNT(*) AS n
                  FROM big GROUP BY country, status ORDER BY n DESC"
```
Two things to watch:
- `frequency` keeps a count for every distinct value in memory. If a column has millions of distinct values, use `sqlp` instead.
- In `sqlp`, the table name is the file name without `.csv` (so `big` above). `_t_1` also works and always refers to the first file.

---

## Alternatives

**DuckDB CLI** (one binary, MIT license): best if you'd rather write SQL for everything. It's very fast at group-bys on multi-GB files and also reads quoted fields correctly.
```bash
# Download duckdb_cli-linux-amd64.zip from https://github.com/duckdb/duckdb/releases, unzip, then:
install -m 755 duckdb ~/.local/bin/
duckdb -c "SELECT country, count(*) n FROM read_csv('big.csv') WHERE status='active' GROUP BY ALL ORDER BY n DESC"
duckdb -c "COPY (SELECT id, country FROM read_csv('big.csv') WHERE status='active') TO 'out.csv' (HEADER)"
```

**Miller (`mlr`)** (one Go binary, BSD license): the only one of the three that's in the standard distro repos, e.g. `sudo apt install miller` or `sudo dnf install miller`. It's slower than qsv or DuckDB on 5 GB files but still far lighter than pandas. Miller 6 reads quoted line breaks correctly.
```bash
mlr --icsv --ocsv filter '$status == "active"' then cut -f id,country big.csv > out.csv
mlr --icsv --opprint count -g country big.csv
```

**Rule of thumb:** use qsv for fast everyday filtering and column picking, DuckDB when the question is easier to write as SQL, and Miller if you're only allowed packages from your distro's repos.

question: q02
text:
I recommend **leakguard**. It's a small Rust command-line tool that reads stdin and writes redacted text to stdout. It runs entirely on your machine, needs no network, and is MIT/Apache-2.0 licensed. You don't write any regexes: it already detects emails, IPv4 and IPv6 addresses, JWTs, AWS, GitHub, Slack, Stripe, Google and OpenAI keys, Azure connection strings, PEM private keys, passwords inside URLs, and more. Version 1.0.0 came out on 2026-10-06 and it has about 74k downloads on crates.io.

I haven't installed or run it. [source], the tool-recommendation service I checked first, had no tested tool for this job. Everything below comes from leakguard's README and its crates.io page.

## Install (Linux)

You need a Rust toolchain (Rust 1.70 or newer). If you don't have one, install it with your distro's package manager or with rustup:

```bash
# Option A: distro package (Debian/Ubuntu example)
sudo apt install cargo

# Option B: rustup (official installer; read the script first if you prefer)
curl --proto '=https' --tlsv1.2 -sSf https://sh.rustup.rs | sh

# Then:
cargo install leakguard
```

The binary goes into `~/.cargo/bin`, so make sure that folder is on your `PATH`.

## First run

```bash
# See what it detects
leakguard --list-kinds

# Scrub a log and copy to clipboard for pasting (X11 / Wayland)
leakguard < server.log | xclip -selection clipboard
leakguard < server.log | wl-copy

# Check what was redacted (summary goes to stderr)
leakguard --stats server.log > clean.log

# Live tail
tail -f app.log | leakguard
```

By default each match is replaced with a label such as `[REDACTED:EMAIL]`. Some useful options:
- `--mask partial --keep 4` keeps the last 4 characters, which helps you tell values apart.
- `--ignore 10.0.0.1,test@example.com` leaves values you know are safe untouched.
- `--redact-word AcmeCorp` or `--redact-literal "..."` also removes your own hostnames, customer names and similar terms.
- `--without credit_card` helps with logs full of numbers. Some long timestamps pass the card checksum and get redacted by mistake.
- `--check` exits with code 1 if anything sensitive is found, so you can use it as a "safe to paste?" check.

## Important limitation

The command-line tool doesn't do high-entropy detection (spotting random-looking strings); only the library has that. In practice it catches tokens with known formats but can **miss custom or unprefixed secrets**, like `Authorization: Bearer <opaque>` or `api_key=abc123...` from your own services. Always look over the output before pasting, and add `--redact-literal` for any secrets you know about. The README calls the tool "best-effort" and says its detectors are conservative.

## Alternatives (not checked in detail)

- **cleansh** (Rust, `cargo install cleansh`): reads stdin and masks emails, IPs, JWT/AWS/GCP tokens, SSH keys and hex secrets. It's newer and much less used (about 2.7k downloads, last release December 2025).
- **ferret-scan** (Go): `--stdin --enable-redaction` writes redacted text to stdout and scores matches by context. It may catch more generic secrets, but it's a bigger tool.
- **redactor** (its30NA) and **redactcli** (PyPI): both are built specifically for cleaning text before pasting it into an AI chat. They're small projects whose quality I haven't checked.

Sources:
- [leakguard on GitHub](https://github.com/ptukovar/leakguard) · [docs.rs](https://docs.rs/crate/leakguard/latest/source/src/bin/leakguard.rs) · [crates.io API](https://crates.io/api/v1/crates/leakguard)
- [cleansh](https://docs.rs/crate/cleansh/0.1.4/source/src/main.rs) · [crates.io API](https://crates.io/api/v1/crates/cleansh)
- [ferret-scan](https://github.com/orshih6/ferret-scan)
- [redactor](https://github.com/its30NA/redactor)
- [redactcli](https://pypi.org/project/redactcli/)
- [rog7/redact](https://github.com/rog7/redact)
- [redactscan PR #8](https://github.com/boktavec/redactscan/pull/8)

question: q20
text:
# Recommendation: you probably don't need a proxy

Ollama already serves an **OpenAI-compatible API** at `http://localhost:11434/v1`. The official `openai` Python package can talk to it directly. You just point the client at that URL. Nothing extra to install.

**Assumptions:** your script uses `openai` v1.x or later and mostly calls `chat.completions` (and maybe `embeddings`), and Ollama runs on the same desktop as the script.

## Steps (no proxy)

1. **Check that Ollama is running and you have a model:**
   ```bash
   systemctl status ollama          # or: curl http://localhost:11434/api/version
   ollama list
   ollama pull llama3.1:8b          # if you don't have one yet; pick any model you like
   ```

2. **Test the OpenAI-compatible endpoint:**
   ```bash
   curl http://localhost:11434/v1/chat/completions \
     -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
     -d '{"model":"llama3.1:8b","messages":[{"role":"user","content":"Say hi"}]}'
   ```

3. **Point your script at Ollama.** The `openai` package reads these environment variables, so if the script creates `OpenAI()` with no arguments you may not need to edit it at all:
   ```bash
   export OPENAI_BASE_URL=http://localhost:11434/v1
   export OPENAI_API_KEY=ollama     # must be set, but Ollama ignores the value
   python your_script.py
   ```
   Or set it in code:
   ```python
   from openai import OpenAI
   client = OpenAI(base_url="http://localhost:11434/v1", api_key="ollama")
   ```

4. **Fix the model name.** If the script asks for `"gpt-4o"`, Ollama will return "model not found". You have two options:
   - Change the model string in the script to a local model, e.g. `"llama3.1:8b"`, or
   - Leave the script alone and create an alias in Ollama:
     ```bash
     ollama cp llama3.1:8b gpt-4o
     ```

### Things to watch for
- **Context length:** Ollama's default context window is smaller than OpenAI's. Long prompts can get cut off without any error. To raise it, set `OLLAMA_CONTEXT_LENGTH=16384` (or similar) in the Ollama service environment with `sudo systemctl edit ollama`, then restart the service.
- **Feature coverage:** chat, streaming, tools/function calling (on models that support it), JSON mode, vision and embeddings all work. Some OpenAI-only features won't: Assistants, file uploads, batch, `logprobs` and some Responses API features. Newer Ollama versions have basic `/v1/responses` support, so update Ollama if your script uses `client.responses`.

## When to add a gateway: LiteLLM Proxy

Install a gateway only if you need things Ollama doesn't do itself: mapping several OpenAI model names to local models in one config file, real API keys, usage logging, or falling back to OpenAI's cloud when a local model fails. In that case, **LiteLLM Proxy** is the standard choice.

**Install** (in a virtualenv, with the version pinned):
```bash
python3 -m venv ~/litellm-venv && source ~/litellm-venv/bin/activate
pip install 'litellm[proxy]==<current-stable-version>'
```
Pin a version you've checked against LiteLLM's GitHub releases and security notes. In 2026 some LiteLLM releases on PyPI were compromised, so don't install the latest version blindly.

**Configure** `~/litellm/config.yaml`:
```yaml
model_list:
  - model_name: gpt-4o                 # name your script asks for
    litellm_params:
      model: ollama_chat/llama3.1:8b   # what actually runs
      api_base: http://localhost:11434
  - model_name: text-embedding-3-small
    litellm_params:
      model: ollama/nomic-embed-text
      api_base: http://localhost:11434
```

**First run:**
```bash
litellm --config ~/litellm/config.yaml --port 4000
# in another shell:
export OPENAI_BASE_URL=http://localhost:4000
export OPENAI_API_KEY=anything     # or a master_key if you set one in the config
python your_script.py
```

## Summary
Start by setting `OPENAI_BASE_URL=http://localhost:11434/v1` and `OPENAI_API_KEY=ollama`, then match the model names. Most scripts work after that with no extra software. Add LiteLLM later only if you need model mapping, keys, logging or cloud fallback.

question: q12
text:
My recommendation is **`mlx_lm.server`**, the server that comes with Apple's own `mlx-lm` package (ml-explore/mlx-lm, MIT license). It meets every requirement you listed. It runs on MLX rather than llama.cpp, runs in the terminal only, is free and open source, and needs no account. It serves an OpenAI-compatible `/v1/chat/completions` endpoint with streaming (`"stream": true` returns `chat.completion.chunk` events), plus `/v1/models`. `--model` accepts either a Hugging Face repo ID or a local folder.

**Other tools I checked:** [source] (a catalog of tools it has test-installed) had nothing that fit. Its three closest matches all run GGUF/llama.cpp, so I'm not recommending any of them. That means nobody actually ran the steps below. They come from the mlx-lm docs (SERVER.md) and what I know about the tool. I didn't run anything on your machine.

**My assumptions:** You're on macOS 14 or later with Python 3.10 or newer, you're happy with `uv` or `pip`, and your editor or tools let you set a custom OpenAI base URL.

## Install

Pick one. `uv` keeps the tool isolated from your system Python:
```bash
# Option A (recommended): uv
brew install uv            # skip if you already have uv
uv tool install mlx-lm     # puts mlx_lm.server, mlx_lm.generate, etc. on your PATH

# Option B: a plain virtualenv
python3 -m venv ~/.venvs/mlx && source ~/.venvs/mlx/bin/activate
pip install -U mlx-lm
```

## First run

1. **Start the server with a model from Hugging Face.** The first run downloads it into `~/.cache/huggingface`. No login is needed for public `mlx-community` models.
   ```bash
   mlx_lm.server --model mlx-community/Qwen2.5-Coder-7B-Instruct-4bit --host 127.0.0.1 --port 8080
   ```
   Or load a local folder of MLX weights (relative paths count from the folder you start the server in):
   ```bash
   mlx_lm.server --model ~/models/my-mlx-model
   ```
   You can turn your own Hugging Face model into MLX format with `mlx_lm.convert --hf-path <repo> -q`.

2. **Check that streaming works** from a second terminal:
   ```bash
   curl -N http://127.0.0.1:8080/v1/chat/completions \
     -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
     -d '{"messages":[{"role":"user","content":"Write a Python hello world"}],"stream":true,"max_tokens":100}'
   ```
   You should see `data: {...chat.completion.chunk...}` lines appear one at a time. Then run `curl http://127.0.0.1:8080/v1/models` to list the available models.

3. **Point your coding tools at it:**
   - Base URL: `http://127.0.0.1:8080/v1`
   - API key: any placeholder string, if the tool insists on one
   - Model: the same repo ID or path you passed to `--model`

## Tips and caveats
- **Security:** Keep it on `127.0.0.1`. The docs say it "only implements basic security checks" and isn't meant for production, so don't bind it to `0.0.0.0` on networks you don't trust.
- **Long contexts:** `--kv-bits 4` saves memory. It also makes the server handle one request at a time, and the docs suggest lowering `--prefill-step-size` when you use it.
- **Model size:** Choose a size that fits your unified memory. A 4-bit 7–14B model is comfortable on 16–32 GB. `mlx-community` on Hugging Face has thousands of ready-made MLX conversions.
- Run `mlx_lm.server --help` for all the options, such as adapters and a draft model for speculative decoding.

## If it falls short
- **mlx-omni-server** (`pip install mlx-omni-server`) is another MLX-based server that also offers Anthropic-style endpoints and more OpenAI endpoints. It's worth trying if a tool needs function or tool calling that `mlx_lm.server` doesn't handle the way you need. I haven't verified it, so check its README before you rely on it.
- I left out LM Studio because it's a GUI app.

Sources:
- [mlx-lm SERVER.md](https://github.com/ml-explore/mlx-lm/blob/main/mlx_lm/SERVER.md)
- [ml-explore/mlx-lm](https://github.com/ml-explore/mlx-lm)

question: q10
text:
# 不用另外裝工具，Git 內建就做得到

Git 本身有字詞級 diff（`--color-words` / `--word-diff`），但預設用空白切詞。中文沒有空白，所以整段被當成一個「詞」，結果還是整段紅綠。只要把切詞規則改成**每個中文字算一個詞、英文單字照舊算一個詞**就行。

以下假設：你用 bash，系統 locale 是 UTF-8，只想改 `.md` 檔的 diff 行為。

## 主要建議：設定一個給 Markdown 用的 diff 規則

### 1. 先直接試（不改任何設定）

在你的 repo 裡執行：

```bash
git diff --color-words=$'[A-Za-z0-9_]+|[^\x80-\xbf[:space:]][\x80-\xbf]*'
```

- `[A-Za-z0-9_]+`：英文、數字、變數名稱維持整個詞比對
- `[^\x80-\xbf[:space:]][\x80-\xbf]*`：抓一個完整的 UTF-8 字元。每個中文字、每個全形標點各算一個詞
- `$'...'` 是 bash 的語法，會把 `\x80` 這類寫法轉成真正的位元組。Git 的正規表達式是逐位元組比對的，所以一定要這樣寫，不能直接寫成 `.`

輸出會是同一行裡只有改到的字變色，例如「我們~~使用~~**採用**這個方法」。

### 2. 覺得可以，就設成永久的

**(a) 全域設定 diff 驅動的切詞規則**（只要設一次）：

```bash
git config --global diff.zh.wordRegex $'[A-Za-z0-9_]+|[^\x80-\xbf[:space:]][\x80-\xbf]*'
```

**(b) 指定讓 `.md` 套用這個規則**。兩種做法擇一：

- 只套用在單一 repo：在 repo 根目錄的 `.gitattributes` 加上
  ```
  *.md diff=zh
  ```
- 套用在所有 repo：
  ```bash
  git config --global core.attributesFile ~/.gitattributes
  echo '*.md diff=zh' >> ~/.gitattributes
  ```

**(c) 加個簡短的 alias**（可選）：

```bash
git config --global alias.wd 'diff --color-words'
```

### 3. 之後的日常用法

```bash
git wd                       # 工作區的改動，逐字顯示
git diff --color-words       # 跟上一行一樣
git diff --word-diff         # 不靠顏色，用 [-刪-]{+增+} 標記，適合貼給別人看或沒有彩色的終端機
git log -p --color-words     # 看歷史紀錄
git show --color-words HEAD
```

設好 `.gitattributes` 之後，`--color-words` 不用再帶正規表達式，會自動用 `diff.zh.wordRegex`。一般的 `git diff` 輸出不變，`git apply` 和 patch 也照常能用。

## 選用：想要更好看的介面可以裝 delta

如果想要並排顯示、語法上色、行號，可以裝 [delta](https://github.com/dandavison/delta)：

```bash
sudo apt install git-delta      # Ubuntu 22.04 以上的套件庫就有
```

`~/.gitconfig` 加上：

```ini
[core]
    pager = delta
[interactive]
    diffFilter = delta --color-only
[delta]
    side-by-side = true
    line-numbers = true
```

要注意的是，delta 預設的行內差異是用 `\w+` 切詞，一整串連續的中文字可能還是會被當成一個詞，標示效果不一定比上面的 Git 內建做法精確。所以建議以 Git 內建的 `--color-words` 為主，delta 是錦上添花，不是必要的。

## 長遠的小建議

如果文件可以接受，寫 Markdown 時每句話換一行（semantic line breaks），渲染結果不變，但一般的 `git diff`、code review 和 merge 衝突都會清楚很多。

question: q01
text:
I recommend **sync-agents-settings**. I didn't install or test any of these tools. I read their READMEs, and [source]'s tested catalog had nothing for this job. I'm assuming you're on macOS with Node.js 18 or newer, and that you add servers with `claude mcp add` already.

## Main pick: sync-agents-settings

It's free (MIT), runs locally with no account, and you can run it from the terminal or inside Claude Code. It doesn't use a separate master file. Your Claude Code config (`~/.claude.json`) is the one list, and the tool copies its MCP servers into:
- Gemini CLI: `~/.gemini/settings.json`, under `mcpServers`
- Codex CLI: `~/.codex/config.toml`

It also supports Cursor, OpenCode, Qwen Code and others, if you add more agents later.

**How it fits what you asked for:**
- **Leaves your other settings alone:** the README's examples show existing settings like theme and model kept next to the synced servers.
- **Safe to test:** `--dry-run` previews the changes, and it backs up each config to `~/.sync-agents-backup/<timestamp>/` before writing.
- **Doesn't create configs:** if one agent's config folder doesn't exist, it skips that agent.

**Main limitation:** it only adds servers that are missing. It never overwrites a server entry that's already in a target, and the README doesn't say it handles removals. So if you change or delete a server in Claude Code, you still have to edit the Gemini and Codex configs by hand.

### Install
```bash
npm install -g sync-agents-settings
```
To try it without installing, use `npx sync-agents-settings list`. You can also install it as a Claude Code plugin, which gives you `/sync`, `/sync-diff` and similar commands:
```bash
claude plugin marketplace add Leoyang183/sync-agents-settings
claude plugin install sync-agents-settings
```

### First run
```bash
sync-agents list                          # show the MCP servers it found in Claude Code
sync-agents diff --target gemini codex    # compare Claude with the other two
sync-agents sync --target gemini --dry-run
sync-agents sync --target codex --dry-run
# if the previews look right:
sync-agents sync --target gemini
sync-agents sync --target codex
```
After that, adding a server looks like this: `claude mcp add …`, then `sync-agents sync --target gemini` and `sync-agents sync --target codex`. To catch drift or parse errors later, run `sync-agents doctor --target gemini codex`.

## Alternatives

- **[mcpport](https://github.com/Abdalkaderdev/mcpport)** (MIT, needs Node 22 or newer): supports Claude Code, Codex, Gemini CLI and Cursor. Usage is `npx mcpport sync <from> <to>`, which is a dry run until you add `--apply`. It backs up each file to `<file>.<timestamp>.bak` before writing and won't write to a file it can't parse. When it writes JSON it keeps keys unrelated to MCP, and when it writes Codex's TOML it keeps your comments and other tables. One catch: it drops server options the target agent doesn't understand, and it lists what it dropped. It copies from one agent to another and has no master file. Try it if you need changes to existing servers carried over, but I couldn't confirm from the README whether it does that.
- **[mcp-sync (Rust)](https://docs.rs/crate/mcp-sync/latest/source/README.md)** (MIT): this one does use a single `mcp.yaml` file as the master list, and it has `--dry-run`, backups and a `watch` mode. But its README lists Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode and Antigravity, **not Gemini CLI**, so it doesn't cover all three of your agents.
- **[mcp-config-manager](https://github.com/holstein13/mcp-config-manager)**: has a sync mode for Claude, Gemini and Codex. But its README gives the Codex config path as `~/.codex.json`, while Codex actually uses `~/.codex/config.toml`. I'd avoid it unless that's been fixed.

I didn't check how actively any of these projects are maintained. Run the dry run before your first real sync either way.

Sources:
- [sync-agents-settings](https://github.com/Leoyang183/sync-agents-settings)
- [mcpport](https://github.com/Abdalkaderdev/mcpport)
- [mcp-sync (Rust crate README)](https://docs.rs/crate/mcp-sync/latest/source/README.md)
- [mcp-sync (EnjoyableWork)](https://github.com/EnjoyableWork/mcp-sync)
- [mcp-sync (PyPI)](https://pypi.org/project/mcp-sync/)
- [mcp-config-manager](https://github.com/holstein13/mcp-config-manager)
- [How to add an MCP server to any AI coding CLI](https://inventivehq.com/blog/add-mcp-server-to-ai-coding-cli)

text:
**Recommendation: mcpup** (`github.com/mohammedsamin/mcpup`). It is a free, MIT-licensed Go CLI that keeps one canonical server list at `~/.mcpup/config.json` and writes into each client's native config. Its client list includes Claude Code and Codex. Its README says "Gemini" without saying Gemini CLI, so confirm that on your first run. It needs no account, and it makes a backup before every write and supports rollback. I couldn't find a last-commit date, and the repo is small (about 24 commits), so treat it as young.

**Fallback: ejfn/mcp-sync**, if mcpup doesn't cover Gemini CLI for you. It reads a Claude-style `mcpServers` file and writes to Claude Code, Gemini CLI, and Codex. Its Codex writer only handles stdio servers. It is run with `uvx --from git+https://github.com/ejfn/mcp-sync mcp-sync -c ~/.claude.json`. I didn't check its backup behavior.

**Install (mcpup, macOS):**
```
brew tap mohammedsamin/tap
brew install mcpup
```
Or, with Go: `go install github.com/mohammedsamin/mcpup/cmd/mcpup@latest`

**First run:**
1. `mcpup setup`, the guided onboarding. It should detect the clients installed on this laptop.
2. `mcpup add <name>` for each server. Add it once to the canonical list.
3. `mcpup enable <name> --client claude-code`, then the same for `codex` and `gemini`. Check `mcpup --help` for the exact client IDs.
4. `mcpup doctor` to check the result.
5. If anything looks wrong, `mcpup rollback --client <client>` restores the backup.

**Before you trust it with your other settings:** back up `~/.codex/config.toml` and `~/.gemini/settings.json` yourself, then diff them after the first sync. I could not confirm from the README that comments and unrelated Codex keys survive a write, so the diff is the check.

I only read READMEs and third-party summaries. I didn't install or run anything.

Sources:
- [mcpup repo](https://github.com/mohammedsamin/mcpup)
- [mcpup listing (mdskills.ai)](https://www.mdskills.ai/mcp-servers/mcpup)
- [ejfn/mcp-sync](https://github.com/ejfn/mcp-sync)
- [EnjoyableWork/mcp-sync](https://github.com/EnjoyableWork/mcp-sync), ruled out because it doesn't support Claude Code or Gemini CLI
- [mcpm (pathintegral-institute)](https://github.com/pathintegral-institute/mcpm.sh/pull/210/files), Gemini and Codex support was only in an open PR when I checked

question: q17
text:
I recommend **Ollama + AIChat**. Both are free and open source, and both work completely offline once the models are downloaded.

- **Ollama** runs a small language model and an embedding model on your CPU.
- **AIChat** (github.com/sigoden/aichat) is a terminal chat tool with document search built in. It indexes your notes and PDFs into a local database, finds the passages that match your question, and passes them to the model. Its `.sources rag` command lists the files each answer came from.

It's a single Rust binary with no Python setup or web interface. I'm assuming you're fine typing questions into a terminal chat prompt and don't need a graphical app.

## Install

1. **Ollama:**
   ```
   curl -fsSL https://ollama.com/install.sh | sh
   ```
   Or use your distro's package or the tarball from ollama.com.

2. **Models.** Download these once while you're online:
   ```
   ollama pull qwen3:4b            # chat model, ~2.5 GB, usable speed on CPU
   ollama pull nomic-embed-text    # embedding model for search
   ```
   With 16 GB RAM and no GPU, a 3–4B model is the practical choice. `qwen3:8b` or `llama3.1:8b` give better answers but are about half as fast. Model names change over time, so check ollama.com/library for current small models if these have moved on.

3. **PDF text extraction:**
   ```
   sudo apt install poppler-utils   # or: dnf install poppler-utils / pacman -S poppler
   ```

4. **AIChat.** Download the Linux binary from github.com/sigoden/aichat/releases and put it on your PATH. Or install it with `cargo install aichat`. Some distros also package it (for example, `pacman -S aichat`).

## Configure

Create `~/.config/aichat/config.yaml`:

```yaml
model: ollama:qwen3:4b
rag_embedding_model: ollama:nomic-embed-text
rag_top_k: 6

clients:
  - type: openai-compatible
    name: ollama
    api_base: http://localhost:11434/v1
    models:
      - name: qwen3:4b
        max_input_tokens: 32768
      - name: nomic-embed-text
        type: embedding
        default_chunk_size: 1500
        max_batch_size: 50

document_loaders:
  pdf: 'pdftotext $1 -'
```

AIChat only talks to Ollama on `localhost`, so nothing leaves your laptop. To check this, turn off Wi-Fi and run a query.

## First run

```
aichat --rag notes
```

1. AIChat asks you to confirm the embedding model, chunk size and overlap. The defaults are fine.
2. When it asks for documents, enter a glob such as:
   ```
   ~/notes/**/*.{md,pdf}
   ```
   Separate multiple paths with `;`.
3. Indexing about 2,000 notes on CPU will probably take somewhere between several minutes and around 30 minutes. It only happens once.
4. Ask questions at the prompt:
   ```
   notes> What did I decide about the backup strategy last spring?
   notes> .sources rag
   ```
   `.sources rag` lists the files and passages used for the last answer.
5. For one-off questions from the shell:
   ```
   aichat --rag notes "summarize my notes on Kubernetes networking"
   ```

**Maintenance:** after adding or editing notes, run `.rebuild rag` inside the session. It re-indexes only what changed.

## Tips and caveats

- **Citations in the answer itself:** you can add an instruction such as "cite the file name for each claim". Small models don't always follow it reliably, so treat `.sources rag` as the authoritative list.
- **Better search results:** add `rag_reranker_model` if you set up a local reranker. The default hybrid search (keyword plus vector) already works well for notes.
- **Scanned PDFs:** these have no text layer, so `pdftotext` returns nothing. Run them through `ocrmypdf` first.
- **Accuracy:** a 4B model sometimes gets details wrong. Check important answers against the cited files.

## Alternatives

- **llm (Simon Willison) + llm-ollama:** good for scripting, but you'd have to build the document search and citations yourself.
- **AnythingLLM** or **Open WebUI:** offline document chat with citations, but through a GUI or browser, not the terminal.
- **PrivateGPT:** more setup (Python), and it's built around an API or web interface.

Source: [AIChat RAG Guide](https://github.com/sigoden/aichat/wiki/RAG-Guide). Some details come from my own knowledge and weren't checked against that page: the Ollama and model install commands, the config keys other than `document_loaders`, and the `.sources rag` and `.rebuild rag` commands. If any of them doesn't work, check the AIChat README or `.help`.

question: q07
text:
Yes, and I'd use **Bruno** for this. It's free and open source under the MIT license. It has no cloud workspace and no sign-in, and it works fully offline. It saves each request as a plain-text `.bru` file in a folder you commit to git, so changes show up as normal diffs in code review. Its CLI (`bru`) runs the same files as tests in Linux CI and exits with a non-zero code when an assertion fails, which fails the build.

I'm assuming you want a desktop app for day-to-day work as well as the CLI. If you only need CLI and CI, see **Hurl** under "Alternatives."

## Install (Mac)

```bash
brew install bruno                 # desktop app (or download the .dmg from usebruno.com)
npm install -g @usebruno/cli       # the `bru` CLI, needs Node.js
```

## First run

1. Open Bruno, choose **Create Collection**, and pick a folder inside your repo, such as `api/`.
2. Add a request. Under **Assert** or **Tests**, add checks. A `.bru` file looks roughly like this:
   ```
   meta { name: Get user  type: http  seq: 1 }
   get { url: {{baseUrl}}/users/1 }
   assert {
     res.status: eq 200
     res.body.id: eq 1
   }
   ```
3. Create an environment, such as `local`, that sets `baseUrl`. Keep secrets out of git: use Bruno's secret variables, or a `.env` file that's in your `.gitignore` and read through `{{process.env.X}}`.
4. Run it locally from the collection folder:
   ```bash
   cd api
   bru run --env local
   ```
5. Commit the folder.

## CI (Linux, GitHub Actions example)

```yaml
- uses: actions/setup-node@v4
  with: { node-version: 20 }
- run: npm install -g @usebruno/cli
- run: bru run --env ci --reporter-junit results.xml
  working-directory: api
```

The step fails if any assertion fails. You can feed `results.xml` to a JUnit test reporter, and the CLI can also write JSON and HTML reports. Bruno also publishes an official GitHub Action.

Things to know:
- In CLI v3, tests run in a restricted "Safe Mode" sandbox by default. If your test scripts use Node built-ins or npm modules, add `--sandbox developer`.
- Pin the CLI version in CI so local and CI behavior stay the same.

## Alternatives
- **[Hurl](https://hurl.dev)** (open source, single Rust binary): it has no GUI, but its `.hurl` text format is very easy to read in diffs, and it was built for CI. Install with `brew install hurl` on Mac or a `.deb`/binary on Linux, then run `hurl --test *.hurl`. Pick this if your team is happy working only in text files.
- **httpyac**: runs `.http` files, the same format as the VS Code and JetBrains REST clients, from a CLI. It's a good fit if your team already uses those editor plugins.

Sources:
- [@usebruno/cli on npm](https://npmjs.com/package/@usebruno/cli)
- [Bruno docs – GitHub Actions overview](https://docs.usebruno.com/bru-cli/github-actions/overview)
- [Bruno docs – GitHub Actions manual setup](https://docs.usebruno.com/bru-cli/github-actions/manual-setup)
- [bruno-cli-action](https://awesome.ecosyste.ms/projects/github.com%2Fusebruno%2Fbruno-cli-action)
- [DEV Community – Bruno CLI vs Apidog CLI](https://dev.to/hassann/bruno-cli-vs-apidog-cli-run-api-tests-in-ci-30cn)

question: q06
text:
**My recommendation is `@ivotoby/openapi-mcp-server`** ([GitHub: ivo-toby/mcp-openapi-server](https://github.com/ivo-toby/mcp-openapi-server)). It's MIT-licensed and runs locally through `npx`. You point it at your OpenAPI spec and your API's base URL, and it turns each operation into an MCP tool. When an agent calls a tool, it sends the HTTP request to your base URL with whatever headers you set. You don't write any server code and you don't need an account or hosted service.

**How I checked:** I read the project's README. I didn't install or test it, and [source] (the catalogue I searched) has no tested tools for this job. The steps below come from the docs and haven't been run on a Mac.

**My assumptions:** macOS with Node.js 18+ available; your agent is Claude Code or Claude Desktop (any MCP client works the same way); your API authenticates with a header such as a bearer token or API key.

## Install and first run

1. **Requirement:** Node.js 18 or later (`brew install node` if you don't have it). Nothing else to install, because `npx` downloads the package on first run.

2. **Test it in your terminal first** using HTTP transport, which makes it easy to check:
   ```bash
   npx -y @ivotoby/openapi-mcp-server \
     --api-base-url https://internal-api.example.corp \
     --openapi-spec ./openapi.yaml \
     --headers "Authorization:Bearer $INTERNAL_API_TOKEN" \
     --transport http --port 3000
   ```
   The server listens on `http://127.0.0.1:3000/mcp`. `--openapi-spec` takes either a file path or a URL. Give it only one spec source, or it exits with an error.

3. **Register it with your agent** using stdio, the default transport, so the agent starts the server itself.

   Claude Code:
   ```bash
   claude mcp add internal-api \
     -e API_BASE_URL=https://internal-api.example.corp \
     -e OPENAPI_SPEC_PATH=/absolute/path/to/openapi.yaml \
     -e API_HEADERS="Authorization:Bearer YOUR_TOKEN" \
     -- npx -y @ivotoby/openapi-mcp-server
   ```
   Claude Desktop, or any client that reads `mcpServers` JSON (on a Mac, Claude Desktop's file is `~/Library/Application Support/Claude/claude_desktop_config.json`):
   ```json
   {
     "mcpServers": {
       "internal-api": {
         "command": "npx",
         "args": ["-y", "@ivotoby/openapi-mcp-server"],
         "env": {
           "API_BASE_URL": "https://internal-api.example.corp",
           "OPENAPI_SPEC_PATH": "/absolute/path/to/openapi.yaml",
           "API_HEADERS": "Authorization:Bearer YOUR_TOKEN"
         }
       }
     }
   }
   ```

4. **First task:** In Claude Code, run `/mcp` to check that `internal-api` is connected and to see its tools. Then ask the agent to call something harmless, like "list the first 5 items using the internal API."

## Useful options
- **Large APIs:** `--tools dynamic` gives the agent just three tools (`list-api-endpoints`, `get-api-endpoint-schema`, `invoke-api-endpoint`) instead of one per operation, which keeps the agent's context small.
- **Limiting what agents can reach:** you can filter by `--tag`, `--exclude-tag`, `--resource /prefix`, `--operation get`, or list exact operations with `--tools explicit --tool <operationId>`. For example, `--operation get` gives you a read-only setup. The docs note that these filters only control which tools exist, not who's allowed to do what, so your API's own auth still has to protect sensitive endpoints.
- **Tokens:** pass your token through an environment variable or your client's env config instead of committing it into a shared config file.

## Alternative: FastMCP (Python)
Pick [FastMCP](https://gofastmcp.com/integrations/openapi) if you want more control, such as mapping some routes to resources instead of tools, excluding routes by regex, or custom auth. It's open source and runs locally, but you have to write a short Python script, so it doesn't strictly meet your "no code" requirement:
```python
import httpx
from fastmcp import FastMCP

client = httpx.AsyncClient(base_url="https://internal-api.example.corp",
                           headers={"Authorization": "Bearer YOUR_TOKEN"})
spec = httpx.get("https://internal-api.example.corp/openapi.json").json()
mcp = FastMCP.from_openapi(openapi_spec=spec, client=client, name="Internal API")

if __name__ == "__main__":
    mcp.run()
```
Install with `uv pip install fastmcp` or `pip install fastmcp`. Then register it with `claude mcp add internal-api -- python /path/to/server.py`. [source] hasn't tested FastMCP either.

**Tip:** whichever tool you use, the tool names and descriptions come from your spec's `operationId`s and summaries. Clear, unique values for those make a big difference to how well agents choose the right call.

Sources:
- https://github.com/ivo-toby/mcp-openapi-server
- https://gofastmcp.com/integrations/openapi

question: q02
text:
**My pick: [leakguard](https://github.com/ptukovar/leakguard).** It's a small Rust command-line tool, dual-licensed MIT/Apache-2.0, with no dependencies. It reads from stdin, writes the redacted text to stdout, and runs entirely on your machine. The patterns are already built in, so you don't write any regexes.

**What it catches by default:** emails, IPv4 and IPv6 addresses, JWTs, AWS, Google, Stripe and OpenAI keys, GitHub, Slack, Telegram and Discord tokens, passwords inside URLs, Azure connection strings, PEM private keys, plus credit cards, SSNs, MAC addresses and IBANs. It can also flag any random-looking string as a possible secret (the generic "high-entropy" detector), but that's off by default and you have to turn it on.

## Install

I'm assuming you have the Rust toolchain or are willing to install it. The tool is installed through Cargo, Rust's package manager.

```bash
# Only if you don't already have cargo (Rust's official installer):
curl --proto '=https' --tlsv1.2 -sSf https://sh.rustup.rs | sh
source "$HOME/.cargo/env"

cargo install leakguard
leakguard --list-kinds    # shows the exact names of the things it can detect
```

## First run

```bash
# 1. Test on a sample first and compare the output with the original
leakguard --stats < server.log > server.redacted.log
diff <(head -200 server.log) <(head -200 server.redacted.log) | less

# 2. Normal use: pipe a log through it
journalctl -u myapp --since "1 hour ago" | leakguard > for-ai.txt
tail -n 500 /var/log/nginx/error.log | leakguard

# 3. Also scrub your own internal hostnames or names it can't know about
cat app.log | leakguard --redact-word mycorp.internal --redact-word db-prod-01
```

Use `--only` and `--without` to choose which patterns run, and `--mask` to change how redacted values look. To turn on the random-string detector, find its exact name in `--list-kinds` and add it with `--only`. If you do that, list the default kinds you still want as well. I haven't checked whether `--only` replaces the default set or adds to it, so look at the output to be sure. `--check` exits with code 1 if it finds anything, which is handy in scripts.

## Caveats

- **It's young.** Version 1.0.0 came out on 2026-10-06 and looks like a one-person project. Read through the source before you trust it, and pin the version.
- **Pattern matching has gaps.** It will miss secrets in formats it doesn't know: custom session IDs, internal hostnames, usernames, and keys inside unusual config formats. Always skim the output before you paste it. `--redact-word` handles known internal strings.
- **IPs:** it redacts all of them, including harmless ones like `127.0.0.1`. If you want to keep some, `--ignore` lets you allowlist values.

## Alternatives

- **[cleansh](https://docs.rs/crate/cleansh/latest)** (Rust, MIT/Apache-2.0): `cargo install cleansh`, then `cat app.log | cleansh sanitize`. It covers similar ground, also shortens home paths to `~/`, and has an opt-in random-string detector (`--engine entropy`). It pulls in an HTTP library and has inactive paid-service stubs. If you need a guarantee that nothing leaves the machine, check the source or run it with no network access.
- **[hexredact](https://github.com/happygream/hexredact):** replaces each value with a token, and the same value always gets the same token. That lets the AI still follow, say, "IP_3" through the whole log, and you can reverse it afterwards.
- **[rog7/redact](https://github.com/rog7/redact)** and **[local-redact](https://github.com/sumankrsh/local-redact)** (Python): simpler, smaller pattern sets.
- Gitleaks and TruffleHog are better known, but they report secrets rather than filtering text through, so they don't fit stdin-to-stdout use.

I didn't install or run any of these. The details above come from their docs.rs and GitHub pages.

Sources:
- [leakguard on docs.rs](https://docs.rs/crate/leakguard/latest) / [source](https://docs.rs/crate/leakguard/latest/source/src/bin/leakguard.rs)
- [cleansh on docs.rs](https://docs.rs/crate/cleansh/latest) / [cleansh crate docs](https://docs.rs/cleansh/0.1.7/i686-unknown-linux-gnu/cleansh/)
- [hexredact](https://github.com/happygream/hexredact)
- [rog7/redact](https://github.com/rog7/redact)
- [local-redact](https://github.com/sumankrsh/local-redact)
