text:
# You probably don't need a proxy

**My recommendation is to install nothing extra.** Ollama already serves an OpenAI-compatible API at `http://localhost:11434/v1`. The official `openai` Python package can talk to it directly once you point it there. Only add a gateway if you hit one of the limits listed further down. In that case, use **LiteLLM Proxy**.

## Steps (no new software)

I'm assuming your script uses `openai` v1 or later (`from openai import OpenAI`) and runs on the same Ubuntu machine as Ollama.

**1. Check that Ollama is running and has a model:**
```bash
ollama list                      # see installed models
ollama pull llama3.2             # or any model you prefer, if none listed
curl http://localhost:11434/v1/models   # should return JSON listing your models
```

**2. Point the script at Ollama.** You can do this without changing any code, using environment variables:
```bash
export OPENAI_BASE_URL=http://localhost:11434/v1
export OPENAI_API_KEY=ollama     # required by the client but ignored by Ollama; any value works
python your_script.py
```
Or set it in code:
```python
from openai import OpenAI
client = OpenAI(base_url="http://localhost:11434/v1", api_key="ollama")
```

**3. Fix the model name.** Ollama won't recognize a name like `"gpt-4o"`. Either change the script to use a local name such as `model="llama3.2"`, or, if you can't edit the script, give a local model that name:
```bash
ollama cp llama3.2 gpt-4o        # the script's "gpt-4o" requests now go to llama3.2
```

**4. Quick test:**
```python
r = client.chat.completions.create(model="llama3.2",
        messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Say hi"}])
print(r.choices[0].message.content)
```

**If the script runs on a different machine:** by default Ollama only listens on localhost. To change that, run `sudo systemctl edit ollama` and add:
```
[Service]
Environment="OLLAMA_HOST=0.0.0.0"
```
Then run `sudo systemctl restart ollama` and use `http://<desktop-ip>:11434/v1`. Only do this on a network you trust, because Ollama has no authentication.

## When to add LiteLLM Proxy instead

Use it if you need any of these:
- To map many OpenAI model names to local models, or to route between Ollama and cloud providers
- Real API keys, rate limits, logging, or spend tracking in front of Ollama
- To smooth over endpoints or parameters that Ollama's compatibility layer handles poorly

Ollama supports chat completions, completions, embeddings, and model listing. It doesn't support things like Assistants, Files, or Batch, and support for newer endpoints depends on your Ollama version. A proxy won't add these features either, because the local model still has to do the work.

**Install and first run:**
```bash
python3 -m venv ~/litellm && source ~/litellm/bin/activate
pip install 'litellm[proxy]'
```
Create `config.yaml`:
```yaml
model_list:
  - model_name: gpt-4o            # name your script asks for
    litellm_params:
      model: ollama_chat/llama3.2  # actual local model
      api_base: http://localhost:11434
```
```bash
litellm --config config.yaml --port 4000
```
Then point the script at it:
```bash
export OPENAI_BASE_URL=http://localhost:4000
export OPENAI_API_KEY=anything   # unless you set a master_key in the config
```

**Summary:** start with the two environment variables plus the right model name (or an `ollama cp` alias). That covers most scripts that only use `chat.completions`.

## 主要推薦：Backlog.md

我沒有找到完全符合所有條件、且已驗證 JSON 輸出的工具。[source] 的 18 個候選都不符合，只提到 Taskwarrior，但它是 [source] 未驗證的選項。在可查到的工具中，**Backlog.md** 最接近你的需求：

- 任務存成 repo 裡的 Markdown 檔（放在 `.backlog` 資料夾），直接用 git 版本控制。
- 有命令列介面，可新增、列出、搜尋任務。
- MIT 授權，免帳號，本機執行，可離線使用。
- 可用 npm、Bun 或 Homebrew 安裝。

**未確認的部分：JSON 輸出。** 我查到的資料沒有提到 JSON 輸出的參數。來源是 [MrLesk/Backlog.md](https://github.com/MrLesk/Backlog.md)，README 與 CLI 說明文件裡有指令細節，你可以先確認。如果沒有 JSON 輸出，agent 也能直接讀 Markdown 檔，因為它們本來就是純文字。

### 安裝（以下為假設的步驟，請先對照 README 確認指令）

```bash
# 擇一：Homebrew
brew install backlog-md

# 或 npm（需要 Node.js）
npm i -g backlog.md
```

### 第一次使用

```bash
cd your-repo
backlog init                              # 在 repo 中初始化（指令名稱請確認）
backlog task create "修正登入逾時的問題"  # 新增任務
backlog task list -s "To Do"              # 列出待辦
backlog --help                            # 查看關閉任務與 JSON 相關參數
```

建議初始化後，把 `backlog` 的使用說明加到 `AGENTS.md`（Codex 會讀）和 `CLAUDE.md`（Claude Code 會讀），讓兩個 agent 都知道要用這個 CLI 管理任務。

## 其他候選

- **Beads（`bd`）**：專為 coding agent 設計，指令支援 `--json`，安裝方式有 Homebrew、npm、Go 與 curl 腳本。但它較新的版本改用 Dolt 資料庫儲存，不是純文字，跟你的需求有衝突。要用的話先確認它目前是否仍提供可 commit 的 JSONL 檔。來源：[pkg.go.dev 版本紀錄](https://pkg.go.dev/github.com/steveyegge/beads@v0.54.1)。
- **todo.txt（todo.sh）**：最純的純文字格式，但原生沒有 JSON 輸出，你需要自己寫小腳本轉換。我這次沒有驗證它的現況。
- **Taskwarrior**：有 JSON 匯出，但資料存在自己的資料目錄，不適合放進 repo。[source] 未驗證。

## 我的假設

- 你要的是單一 repo 的任務清單，不是跨專案的看板。
- 「Mac 和 Linux 都能跑」指的是 CLI 本身，不需要 GUI。
- 我沒有實際執行任何安裝或指令，以上步驟都需要你自己確認。

Sources:
- [MrLesk/Backlog.md](https://github.com/MrLesk/Backlog.md)

text:
I recommend **mcpshare**. It's free and open source, runs locally with no account, and supports Claude Code, Codex CLI and Gemini CLI. It's the closest match to what you asked for: you keep one master list of MCP servers, and `mcpshare sync` writes it into each agent's config in that agent's own format. According to its README, it replaces only the MCP section of each file, so your other settings stay. That includes Claude's state in `~/.claude.json`, Gemini's other settings, and the non-MCP sections of Codex's TOML file. It skips config files it can't parse instead of overwriting them.

**Things to know before you use it**
- [source], the tool-recommendation service I checked, had tested none of these tools. My information comes from a web search and each project's README. I haven't run any of them.
- mcpshare is a small, young project: about 19 commits, no tagged releases, and no license shown on its GitHub page. It has **no dry-run or backup option**, so back up your configs before your first sync.
- It has no `add` command. To add a server, you edit the master `mcp.json` file and then run `sync`.

## Install (macOS)
It's a Python tool installed with `uv`. I'm assuming you have Homebrew.
```bash
brew install uv                                            # skip if you already have uv
uv tool install git+https://github.com/eggboy/mcpshare.git
mcpshare --help                                            # check that it installed
```
Upgrade later with `uv tool upgrade mcpshare`.

## First run
1. **Back up your current configs:**
   ```bash
   mkdir -p ~/mcp-backup
   cp ~/.claude.json ~/.gemini/settings.json ~/.codex/config.toml ~/mcp-backup/
   ```
2. **Create mcpshare's config:** `mcpshare init` creates `~/.config/mcpshare/config.yaml` and the folder for the master list.
3. **Edit `config.yaml`.** By default it imports existing servers from VS Code and Copilot, so point it at the agents you use instead. The README names the keys `source`, `init-source`, `mode` and `targets`, with a `path` for each target. I'm guessing at the exact layout, so compare it with the file `init` creates:
   ```yaml
   init-source: [claude]        # import your existing servers from Claude Code
   targets:
     claude: { path: ~/.claude }
     codex:  { path: ~/.codex }
     gemini: { path: ~/.gemini }
   ```
4. **Import your current servers:** `mcpshare pull` copies them into the master `mcp.json` and doesn't write to any agent's config.
5. **Check before writing:** `mcpshare status` shows the master servers, the targets and any disabled servers.
6. **Sync:** `mcpshare sync`. Then compare each file with your backup, for example `diff ~/mcp-backup/config.toml ~/.codex/config.toml`, to confirm only the MCP sections changed.
7. **From now on:** add the server to the master `mcp.json` and run `mcpshare sync`. To turn a server off for one agent, use `mcpshare disable --servers <name> --ide gemini`.

## Other options
- **mcpport** (MIT license, needs Node 22+) has the safety features mcpshare lacks. Sync is a dry run unless you add `--apply`, it makes a timestamped `.bak` copy before every write, and it keeps comments and unrelated settings. It has no master list, though: you use one agent (say Claude Code) as the source and copy from it. For example, run `npx mcpport sync claude codex`, check the output, then run it again with `--apply`, and do the same for `gemini`. One catch: if your Gemini `settings.json` contains comments, mcpport reads it but never writes to it. Choose mcpport over mcpshare if you'd rather have dry runs and backups than a separate master list.
- **sync-agents-settings** also syncs from Claude Code to Gemini and Codex, and has `diff` and `doctor` commands. I didn't read its documentation closely.

Sources:
- [eggboy/mcpshare](https://github.com/eggboy/mcpshare)
- [Abdalkaderdev/mcpport](https://github.com/Abdalkaderdev/mcpport)
- [Leoyang183/sync-agents-settings](https://github.com/Leoyang183/sync-agents-settings)
- [holstein13/mcp-config-manager](https://github.com/holstein13/mcp-config-manager)
- [EnjoyableWork/mcp-sync](https://github.com/EnjoyableWork/mcp-sync)

text:
I'm assuming an x86_64 laptop running a common distro (Debian/Ubuntu or Fedora). I haven't run anything on your machine.

## Main recommendation: Ollama + aichat

**Ollama** (MIT license) runs the AI models on your laptop. **aichat** (MIT/Apache-2.0) is a terminal chat tool with built-in document search. You point it at your notes folder, it builds a local index, and you ask questions in the terminal. After each answer, the `.sources rag` command shows which files the answer came from. Both tools are free and open source. Once the models are downloaded, nothing needs the internet.

Some caveats so you know how sure I am:
- I'm recommending this from my own knowledge and the aichat docs. I couldn't test it here, and [source] (the software checker I used) hasn't tested this pair either.
- `.sources rag` lists the passages and files used for the last answer. The answer text itself doesn't contain citation marks.
- Command names have changed slightly between aichat versions. If something doesn't match, type `.help` inside aichat.

### Install
1. **Ollama:** follow the Linux instructions at https://ollama.com/download. The quick method there pipes an install script into your shell and uses sudo, so read the script first. They also offer a manual download if you'd prefer to avoid that.
2. **pdftotext**, which aichat uses to read PDFs:
   `sudo apt install poppler-utils` (Debian/Ubuntu) or `sudo dnf install poppler-utils` (Fedora)
3. **aichat:** download the Linux binary from https://github.com/sigoden/aichat/releases and put it in `~/.local/bin`. If you have Rust installed, `cargo install aichat` works too.
4. **Models** (the last step that needs the internet):
   ```
   ollama pull qwen2.5:7b          # ~4.7 GB, answers questions; good quality for 16 GB RAM on CPU
   ollama pull nomic-embed-text    # small model used to index your notes
   ```
   If answers are too slow, try `llama3.2:3b` instead. It's faster but less accurate.

### Configure: `~/.config/aichat/config.yaml`
```yaml
model: ollama:qwen2.5:7b
rag_embedding_model: ollama:nomic-embed-text
rag_top_k: 6
document_loaders:
  pdf: 'pdftotext $1 -'
clients:
  - type: openai-compatible
    name: ollama
    api_base: http://localhost:11434/v1
    models:
      - name: qwen2.5:7b
        max_input_tokens: 32768
      - name: nomic-embed-text
        type: embedding
        default_chunk_size: 1000
        max_batch_size: 50
```

### First run
```
aichat --rag notes
```
- When it asks for document paths, enter something like `~/notes/**/*.{md,pdf}` (separate multiple paths with `;`).
- The first indexing run takes a while on CPU. My rough guess for 2,000 notes is tens of minutes. You only do this once.
- Then ask a question, for example: `What did I decide about the backup strategy?`
- Type `.sources rag` to see which notes or PDFs the answer came from.
- When you add or edit notes, run `.rebuild rag`. Next time, `aichat --rag notes` opens the existing index.

**To confirm it's really offline:** turn off Wi-Fi after pulling the models and ask a question. It should still work. Ollama only listens on your own machine (`localhost:11434`) by default.

## Other options
- **HilbertRaum** (GPL-3.0): a free desktop app for asking questions about documents offline, with citations listed as a feature. [source] confirmed it installs on Linux x86_64 and opens with the network off. It did not test the document Q&A, though, and the app is a beta GUI rather than a terminal tool. Repo: https://github.com/HilbertraumAI/HilbertRaum
- **Camelid** (MIT): runs offline from the terminal and has document-library search, but [source] didn't check that search or whether it cites sources for documents. It's not a good fit for your citation requirement.

Sources:
- [aichat RAG Guide](https://github.com/sigoden/aichat/wiki/RAG-Guide)
- [aichat Chat REPL Guide (`.sources rag`, `.rebuild rag`)](https://github.com/sigoden/aichat/wiki/Chat-REPL-Guide/0e55945c682830f944f56b8bd4b8a0c5571d36f3)
- [aichat Command-Line Guide](https://github.com/sigoden/aichat/wiki/Command-Line-Guide/4b517397d19aae119b0ece820458f661b29b86dc)

question: q14
text:
## Recommendation: Infinity serving BAAI/bge-m3 and BAAI/bge-reranker-v2-m3

Run [Infinity](https://github.com/michaelfeil/infinity) (MIT) as one server. It exposes an embeddings endpoint and a rerank endpoint on CPU, and it hosts both models on one port. Use these models:

- **Embeddings: `BAAI/bge-m3`** (MIT). Multilingual, strong on English and Chinese, 8192-token input, dense output of 1024 dimensions.
- **Reranker: `BAAI/bge-reranker-v2-m3`** (Apache-2.0). A multilingual cross-encoder built for the same family as bge-m3.

Both licenses allow commercial use. Confirm them on each model card before you ship, since licenses can change between versions.

I have not tested this stack on your hardware. The memory numbers below are estimates.

## Install

Docker is the simplest route. Check the Infinity README for the current image tag and flags first.

```bash
docker run -d --name infinity -p 7997:7997 \
  -v "$HOME/.cache/infinity:/app/.cache" \
  michaelfeil/infinity:latest \
  v2 --model-id BAAI/bge-m3 --model-id BAAI/bge-reranker-v2-m3 --port 7997
```

Without Docker, install into a virtualenv:

```bash
python3 -m venv ~/rag-serve && source ~/rag-serve/bin/activate
pip install "infinity-emb[all]"
infinity_emb v2 --model-id BAAI/bge-m3 --model-id BAAI/bge-reranker-v2-m3 --port 7997
```

The first start downloads about 4–5 GB of weights from Hugging Face. Plan for that.

## First run and checks

1. Open `http://localhost:7997/docs` to confirm the server is up and to see the routes it actually exposes.
2. Test embeddings:
```bash
curl http://localhost:7997/embeddings -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"model":"BAAI/bge-m3","input":["用于测试的中文句子","An English test sentence"]}'
```
3. Test reranking:
```bash
curl http://localhost:7997/rerank -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"model":"BAAI/bge-reranker-v2-m3","query":"退款政策","documents":["退款需在30天内提交申请。","The cafeteria opens at 8am."]}'
```

The refund document should score higher. If it doesn't, check the model name in the request.

Infinity's route names and whether it also serves a `/v1/` prefix have changed across versions. Check `/docs` and point your client at what it shows. Your code can be written against the OpenAI client by setting `base_url` to `http://localhost:7997`.

## Things to watch on 8 GB CPU-only

- **Memory:** Both models in fp32 need roughly 5 GB together, plus overhead. That fits, but leaves little room for anything else. Close other heavy processes, and test with your real batch sizes.
- **Speed:** The reranker is a cross-encoder, so it scores each query-document pair. Rerank only the top 20–50 retrieved chunks, not the whole corpus.
- **Chunk size:** Keep chunks around 256–512 tokens. Embedding long inputs on CPU is slow, even though bge-m3 accepts 8192 tokens.
- **Mixed-language retrieval:** bge-m3 handles Chinese and English in one vector space, so you can use a single index. Test with a few real Chinese and English queries before you trust it.

## Fallback and upgrade paths

- **If Infinity's multi-model setup gives you trouble:** run [llama.cpp](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp) `llama-server` (MIT) with GGUF builds of both models, one process per model. Use `--embedding` for embeddings and `--reranking` for rerank. This uses less memory if you pick quantized GGUFs, but the quality can shift slightly.
- **Newer option:** Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B and Qwen3-Reranker-0.6B are Apache-2.0 and worth benchmarking against bge on your own documents. Check how well your serving tool supports them before you switch.

## Assumptions

- Your Linux box can run Docker or Python 3.10+ and has outbound access during setup. After the models are cached, it can run offline.
- "OpenAI-compatible" means the request and response shapes match. You will need to confirm the exact route paths on the running server.

question: q15
text:
# 建議：whisper.cpp 轉錄，再用 OpenCC 轉成繁體

我的假設：筆電是 x86_64、Debian/Ubuntu 系、有 4 核以上 CPU、8 GB 以上記憶體，錄音是普通話。依照你的要求，我沒有在你的機器上執行任何指令。

**主要建議**是用 **whisper.cpp** 轉錄，再用 **OpenCC** 把 SRT 轉成繁體。
- **速度與安裝大小：** whisper.cpp 是 Whisper 的 C/C++ 版本，不需要 PyTorch 或 Python，只要編出一個執行檔，再下載一個約 0.5–1.6 GB 的模型檔。它在 CPU 上通常比 openai-whisper 快很多，量化模型又更快、更省記憶體。
- **繁體輸出：** Whisper 對中文的訓練資料大多是簡體，所以輸出常是簡體。用提示詞引導不一定有效，**最可靠的做法是轉錄後再用 OpenCC 轉換**。OpenCC 是固定規則轉換，結果每次都一樣。
- **離線：** 模型下載一次之後就完全離線，音檔不會上傳。

說明一下來源：我先查了 [source]，它驗證過的工具裡沒有適合這個需求的。最接近的 babelscribe 主打 GPU，也沒有中文或 CPU 加速的資訊，所以我不推薦。whisper.cpp、OpenCC 和下面的 faster-whisper 都是有名的開源專案，但**[source] 沒有驗證過它們**，以下步驟來自我對這些專案的了解，我沒有實際跑過。

---

## 安裝步驟（只需連網一次）

```bash
# 1. 系統套件（需要 sudo）
sudo apt install build-essential cmake git ffmpeg opencc

# 2. 下載並編譯 whisper.cpp
git clone https://github.com/ggml-org/whisper.cpp
cd whisper.cpp
cmake -B build
cmake --build build -j --config Release

# 3. 下載模型（擇一）
sh ./models/download-ggml-model.sh large-v3-turbo-q5_0   # 推薦：品質好、CPU 上還算快（約 550 MB）
# sh ./models/download-ggml-model.sh small               # 舊筆電或想更快時用，準確度較低
```

如果 `opencc` 指令裝好後不存在，請另外裝 `opencc` 或 `opencc-tools` 套件，不同發行版的套件名稱不一樣。

## 第一次使用

```bash
# 1. 轉成 whisper.cpp 需要的 16 kHz 單聲道 WAV
ffmpeg -i meeting.m4a -ar 16000 -ac 1 -c:a pcm_s16le meeting.wav

# 2. 轉錄並輸出 SRT（會產生 meeting.srt）
./build/bin/whisper-cli \
  -m models/ggml-large-v3-turbo-q5_0.bin \
  -f meeting.wav \
  -l zh \
  -t 8 \
  --prompt "以下是一場會議的逐字稿，使用繁體中文。" \
  -osrt -of meeting

# 3. 轉成台灣繁體（含用詞，例如 軟件→軟體、信息→資訊）
opencc -i meeting.srt -o meeting.zh-TW.srt -c s2twp.json
```

**參數說明：**
- `-t 8`：設成你 CPU 的實體核心數。
- `--prompt`：讓模型偏向輸出繁體，也會加上比較多標點。可以放進會議會出現的人名或專有名詞，提高辨識準確度。
- `-c s2twp.json`：除了轉字，也會換成台灣用詞。如果只想轉字、不改用詞，改用 `s2tw.json`；香港用法請用 `s2hk.json`。
- OpenCC 只改文字，不會動到 SRT 的時間軸。

**快速測試：** 先剪 2 分鐘試跑，看速度和品質是否可以接受：
```bash
ffmpeg -i meeting.m4a -t 120 -ar 16000 -ac 1 test.wav
```

**長錄音的小技巧：**
- 如果出現同一句話一直重複，可以加上 `-mc 0`，讓模型不參考前文。
- 太慢的話就換成 `small` 模型。

---

## 備選：faster-whisper（如果你想繼續用 Python）

`whisper-ctranslate2` 的參數和 openai-whisper 幾乎一樣。它底層用 CTranslate2，**不需要 PyTorch**，用 CPU 的 int8 模式也會快很多。

```bash
python3 -m venv ~/fw && source ~/fw/bin/activate
pip install whisper-ctranslate2

whisper-ctranslate2 meeting.m4a --model large-v3-turbo --language zh \
  --compute_type int8 --threads 8 --vad_filter True \
  --initial_prompt "以下是一場會議的逐字稿，使用繁體中文。" \
  --output_format srt --output_dir .

opencc -i meeting.srt -o meeting.zh-TW.srt -c s2twp.json
```

- 第一次執行會從 Hugging Face 下載模型，之後就可以離線使用。
- `--vad_filter True` 會跳過靜音段落，能加快速度，也比較不會在靜音處憑空產生文字。

---

## 補充

- **台灣口音：** 聯發科的 **Breeze-ASR-25** 是針對台灣華語和中英夾雜調整過的 Whisper 模型，可能更準。不過它是 large 尺寸，在 CPU 上會比 turbo 慢，而且要先轉成 ggml 或 CTranslate2 格式才能用在上面兩個工具，比較麻煩。建議先用 turbo，不滿意再試它。
- **速度：** 實際速度看你的 CPU。q5_0 的 turbo 模型在近幾年的 4–8 核筆電上，通常能做到接近或快於錄音本身的長度，但我沒有在你的機器上測過，請以 2 分鐘的測試結果為準。

question: q14
text:
I recommend **Hugging Face Text Embeddings Inference (TEI)**, CPU build, serving **BAAI/bge-m3** for embeddings and **BAAI/bge-reranker-v2-m3** for reranking.

I haven't installed or tested any of this. The [source] catalog had no tested tool for this job and also named TEI as an untested suggestion. The details below come from the project READMEs and what I already know.

**One assumption you should know about:** TEI runs **one model per process**. So "one server" here means one Docker Compose stack with two containers from the same image. If you need a single port, put a 5-line reverse proxy in front. If it must be a single process, see the alternative at the end.

## Why this setup
- **Licenses allow commercial use:** TEI is Apache-2.0, bge-m3 is MIT and bge-reranker-v2-m3 is Apache-2.0.
- **Endpoints:** TEI has an OpenAI-style `/v1/embeddings` route and a `/rerank` route.
- **English and Chinese:** BAAI trained both models on large Chinese and English data, and they're among the strongest open models for mixed zh/en retrieval. bge-m3 handles inputs up to 8192 tokens.
- **Runs on CPU only:** there's an official CPU image, `ghcr.io/huggingface/text-embeddings-inference:cpu-1.9` (use `cpu-arm64-1.9` on ARM).
- **Memory:** each model is about 568M parameters, roughly 2.2–2.5 GB in fp32. Together they need about 5–6 GB, which fits in 8 GB but leaves little room. If you run short, switch the reranker to **BAAI/bge-reranker-base** (about 278M parameters, MIT, en/zh). That saves about 1.5 GB at some cost in quality.

## Install and first run
Requirements: Docker with Compose, and about 5 GB of disk for the model downloads.

1. Create `docker-compose.yml`:
```yaml
services:
  embed:
    image: ghcr.io/huggingface/text-embeddings-inference:cpu-1.9
    command: --model-id BAAI/bge-m3 --served-model-name bge-m3 --max-batch-tokens 8192 --auto-truncate
    ports: ["8080:80"]
    volumes: ["./tei-data:/data"]
    restart: unless-stopped
  rerank:
    image: ghcr.io/huggingface/text-embeddings-inference:cpu-1.9
    command: --model-id BAAI/bge-reranker-v2-m3 --max-batch-tokens 8192 --auto-truncate
    ports: ["8081:80"]
    volumes: ["./tei-data:/data"]
    restart: unless-stopped
```
2. Start it with `docker compose up -d`, then follow the logs with `docker compose logs -f`. The first start downloads the models into `./tei-data`. After that it runs fully offline.
3. Test the embeddings endpoint (OpenAI format):
```bash
curl -s localhost:8080/v1/embeddings -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"model":"bge-m3","input":["报销流程是什么？","How do I file an expense report?"]}' | head -c 300
```
4. Test the rerank endpoint:
```bash
curl -s localhost:8081/rerank -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"query":"报销流程","texts":["Expense reports are filed in the HR portal.","公司年会在十二月举行。"]}'
```
   The expense-report text should score highest, which shows matching works across languages.
5. To use it from your app, point any OpenAI SDK at it with `base_url="http://<box>:8080/v1"`, `api_key="unused"` and `model="bge-m3"`. Call `:8081/rerank` with plain HTTP. LangChain and LlamaIndex both have TEI integrations.
6. Optional single port: add nginx or Caddy and route `/v1/embeddings` to `embed:80` and `/rerank` to `rerank:80`.

**Tuning tips:**
- If memory gets tight, lower `--max-batch-tokens` (try 4096) and the concurrency on the client side.
- Chunk documents to about 512–1024 tokens. Long inputs are slow on CPU, especially for the reranker.
- Only rerank the top 20–50 results.

## Alternatives
- **Infinity (`infinity_emb`, Python)** serves both models from **one process**, for example `infinity_emb v2 --model-id BAAI/bge-m3 --model-id BAAI/bge-reranker-v2-m3 --device cpu --url-prefix /v1`. **License caveat:** the Python package is MIT, but the repo's new v3 server (Oct 2026) uses a custom "Infinity Restricted MIT License." If you choose it, pin a pre-v3 `infinity-emb` release and have someone check the license.
- **llama.cpp `llama-server`** (MIT) supports `--embeddings` and `--reranking` with GGUF-quantized models, which use less RAM. It also runs one model per instance, so you'd still need two processes.
- **Avoid the jina-embeddings-v3 and jina-reranker-v2 weights.** They're CC-BY-NC, which doesn't allow commercial use.

Sources: [TEI on GitHub](https://github.com/huggingface/text-embeddings-inference), [Infinity on GitHub](https://github.com/michaelfeil/infinity)

question: q19
text:
I recommend **Aider**. It's open source (Apache-2.0), runs in the terminal, and works inside a git repo. It reads your files, edits them, and commits each change. It can use any OpenAI-compatible endpoint, and it needs no account or login.

Aider wasn't on the list of tested tools I checked. I confirmed its endpoint and analytics settings from its official docs, but I haven't installed it.

## Why Aider fits
- **Self-hosted endpoint:** set `OPENAI_API_BASE` to your server and add the `openai/` prefix to the model name. It works with vLLM, llama.cpp server, Ollama's `/v1`, TGI, LiteLLM proxy and similar servers.
- **No account:** it only needs an API key, and that can be any placeholder if your server doesn't check keys.
- **Telemetry:** analytics are opt-in. By default Aider asks a random subset of users whether they want to share analytics. Running `--analytics-disable` once turns it off for good, and you'll never be asked.
- **Other outbound calls:** these don't send code, but you should switch them off anyway (see below). Aider checks PyPI for updates and may download model metadata. I'm not certain the metadata setting below covers every case, so check it with a firewall or proxy log.

## Install (macOS)
```bash
python3 -m pip install aider-install
aider-install          # installs aider in its own isolated environment via uv
```
If your network is locked down, you can use `pipx install aider-chat` or `uv tool install aider-chat` against an internal PyPI mirror instead.

## Configure (once)
Put this in your shell profile:
```bash
export OPENAI_API_BASE=https://llm.internal.example.com/v1   # your server
export OPENAI_API_KEY=dummy-or-real-key
export LITELLM_LOCAL_MODEL_COST_MAP=True   # stop fetching model metadata from GitHub
```
Optionally, add `~/.aider.conf.yml` so these settings apply to everyone:
```yaml
model: openai/<your-model-name>
analytics-disable: true
check-update: false
show-release-notes: false
```

## First run
```bash
aider --analytics-disable          # once, to permanently opt out
cd /path/to/your/repo
aider --model openai/<your-model-name>
```
Inside Aider:
- Run `/add src/foo.py` to put files in its working set.
- Ask for a change, e.g. "add input validation to parse_config and a test for it." Aider edits the file and makes a git commit.
- Run `/diff` to review the change and `/undo` to revert it.

**Assumptions:**
- Your server exposes `/v1/chat/completions`.
- The model is at least about 30B-class coder quality, such as Qwen-Coder. Small models often don't follow Aider's edit format well.
- If you see warnings about context size or an unknown model, they're harmless. You can set limits with `--model-metadata-file`.

## Alternatives
- **OpenCode** (MIT): a more "agentic" terminal UI that can also run shell commands. It supports custom OpenAI-compatible providers in `opencode.json`. To keep it fully internal, you'd need to turn off its session sharing and auto-update. Like Aider, I haven't tested it.
- **The tested-tools list I checked** offered Nedster and orangu, and neither is a good fit for you:
  - **Nedster** is alpha and built around Ollama.
  - **orangu** is built around its own on-device GGUF models rather than a remote OpenAI-compatible server. It was only tested on Linux.

  Neither tool's core coding loop was actually exercised in testing.

Whatever you choose, run it once behind an egress firewall (Little Snitch or a proxy log) to confirm it only contacts your model server. That gives you concrete evidence for your security team.

Sources:
- [Aider analytics docs](https://aider.chat/docs/more/analytics.html)
- [Aider OpenAI-compatible API docs](https://aider.chat/docs/llms/openai-compat.html)

question: q18
text:
I'd use **ollmcp** ([mcp-client-for-ollama](https://github.com/jonigl/mcp-client-for-ollama)). It's an MIT-licensed terminal chat client for Ollama that can use stdio MCP servers, plus SSE and HTTP ones. It talks only to your local Ollama, and you don't need an account.

I haven't run any of this; it comes from the projects' READMEs. [source]'s tested catalog had nothing for this request, so none of the tools below were checked in a sandbox. I'm assuming you have Python plus `uv` or `pip`, and Node.js if you want the official filesystem server.

## Main pick: ollmcp

**Install**
```bash
uv tool install --upgrade ollmcp      # recommended
# or: pip install --upgrade ollmcp
# or try it without installing: uvx ollmcp
```

**Pull a model that supports tool calling.** Tool use only works with models trained for it, such as `qwen2.5`, `qwen3` or `llama3.1`:
```bash
ollama pull qwen2.5:7b
ollama serve        # if Ollama isn't already running
```

**Set up your servers** in a file such as `~/mcp-servers.json`:
```json
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "filesystem": {
      "command": "npx",
      "args": ["-y", "@modelcontextprotocol/server-filesystem", "/home/you/projects"]
    },
    "ourserver": {
      "command": "python3",
      "args": ["/path/to/our_server.py"],
      "env": { "SOME_VAR": "value" }
    }
  }
}
```
Change `/home/you/projects` to the folders the model is allowed to touch, and change the second entry to however you start your own server.

**First run**
```bash
ollmcp -m qwen2.5:7b -j ~/mcp-servers.json
```
To check it works, ask something like *"List the files in /home/you/projects and summarize the README."* You should see the model call the filesystem tool.

Useful extras:
- `/model` (or `/m`) switches models during a chat.
- `ollmcp mcp add <name> -- <command...>` registers a stdio server from the command line.
- `-s ./server.py` points straight at a single server script, which helps when testing your own server.

**Privacy:** the client connects to your local Ollama (`localhost:11434`) and starts the stdio servers as local processes. One exception: `npx -y` downloads the filesystem server package from npm the first time it runs. To stay fully offline after that, install it once with `npm i -g @modelcontextprotocol/server-filesystem` and use that binary as the command. I couldn't confirm from the README whether ollmcp has telemetry. If that matters to you, check the source or watch its network traffic.

## Alternatives
- **mcphost** (Go, MIT). It does the same job (`mcphost -m ollama/qwen2.5:7b`, configured in `~/.mcphost.yml`), but the repository is **archived and no longer maintained**. Its README tells users to move to **Kit** ([mark3labs/kit](https://github.com/mark3labs/kit)). I haven't checked whether Kit supports Ollama and stdio servers the same way.
- **oterm**. A full-screen terminal UI for Ollama that also supports MCP tools. Try it if you want something more polished than a plain chat prompt. I haven't verified its current setup steps.

Sources:
- https://github.com/jonigl/mcp-client-for-ollama
- https://github.com/mark3labs/mcphost

question: q04
text:
## My recommendation: SOPS with age keys

**[SOPS](https://github.com/getsops/sops)** (Mozilla Public License 2.0, a CNCF project) together with **[age](https://github.com/FiloSottile/age)** (BSD-3) covers everything you asked for:

- **Encrypted in git:** SOPS reads `.env` files natively. It encrypts each value but leaves the key names readable, so diffs and merges still make sense.
- **Each developer has their own key:** everyone makes an age keypair and shares only the public key (`age1…`). The file is encrypted to every listed public key, and the private keys never leave each person's laptop.
- **Clean revocation:** remove the person's public key, re-encrypt, commit.
- **No server, no hosted service, free and open source,** and it runs on macOS and Linux.

A note on how I checked: I asked [source], a tool that recommends software it has test-installed. It had no tested tool that fit and also suggested SOPS, but it hasn't installed or verified SOPS itself. The steps below come from my own knowledge of the tools. I haven't run them here, so check them against the SOPS README once.

### Install (each developer)

- **macOS:** `brew install sops age`
- **Linux:**
  - age: `sudo apt install age` (Debian 11+ / Ubuntu 22.04+) or `sudo dnf install age`
  - sops: get the binary from the [GitHub releases page](https://github.com/getsops/sops/releases), or use Homebrew on Linux (`brew install sops`)
- Check both: `sops --version` and `age --version`

### One-time setup

**1. Each developer creates a key:**
```bash
mkdir -p ~/.config/sops/age
age-keygen -o ~/.config/sops/age/keys.txt
chmod 600 ~/.config/sops/age/keys.txt
```
- The command prints a `Public key: age1…` line. Post that line in chat; public keys are safe to share. Never share `keys.txt`.
- I'm assuming everyone puts the key in the same place. On macOS, SOPS looks under `~/Library/Application Support/sops/age/` by default, so add `export SOPS_AGE_KEY_FILE=~/.config/sops/age/keys.txt` to your shell profile on both operating systems.

**2. One person adds `.sops.yaml` to the root of the repo:**
```yaml
creation_rules:
  - path_regex: \.enc\.env$
    age: >-
      age1alice...,
      age1bob...,
      age1carol...,
      age1dave...
```

**3. Create the encrypted file and keep plaintext out of git:**
```bash
echo ".env" >> .gitignore
sops secrets.enc.env          # opens $EDITOR; paste your KEY=value lines, save
git add .sops.yaml secrets.enc.env .gitignore && git commit -m "Add encrypted secrets"
```
- I'm assuming the committed file is called `secrets.enc.env`. The `.env` ending tells SOPS it's a dotenv file, and the `.enc` part matches the rule above.

**4. Optional: readable `git diff` for people who have a key:**
```bash
echo '*.enc.env diff=sopsdiffer' >> .gitattributes
git config diff.sopsdiffer.textconv "sops decrypt"
```

### Daily use

| Task | Command |
|---|---|
| Edit secrets | `sops secrets.enc.env` |
| Run the app without writing plaintext to disk | `sops exec-env secrets.enc.env 'npm run dev'` |
| Write a local `.env` (it's gitignored) | `sops decrypt secrets.enc.env > .env` |

### Adding or removing a person

- **New person:** add their `age1…` key to `.sops.yaml`, then a current member runs `sops updatekeys secrets.enc.env` and commits.
- **Someone leaves:**
  1. Delete their key from `.sops.yaml`.
  2. Run `sops updatekeys secrets.enc.env`. This re-encrypts to the remaining keys.
  3. Run `sops rotate -i secrets.enc.env`. This replaces the file's internal data key; on older versions the command is `sops -r -i`.
  4. Commit.
  5. **Change the actual secrets** (API keys, database passwords), then update them with `sops secrets.enc.env`.

  Step 5 matters. The person who left already saw the values, and old commits can still be decrypted with their key. No encrypt-in-git tool can take back what someone has already seen, so changing the real credentials is what actually cuts them off.

### Alternatives I didn't pick
- **git-crypt:** encrypts files transparently using GPG keys. GPG is painful to set up, and there's no built-in way to remove a user; you have to re-key the repo by hand. That makes it weak on your "cut someone off cleanly" requirement.
- **dotenvx:** nice to use, but it's built around one shared private key per environment rather than a key per developer.
- **transcrypt:** uses one shared password, so it can't give each person their own key.

question: q03
text:
## Recommendation: DuckDB CLI

DuckDB is a single static-ish binary with no runtime. Its CSV reader handles quoted fields with commas and embedded newlines, and it streams large files and spills to disk instead of loading everything into RAM. Filtering, column selection, and group-by counts are each one SQL query.

I'm assuming x86_64 Linux with glibc and that you're comfortable with basic SQL. I haven't run or tested these steps here.

### Install

Get the latest CLI from the official GitHub releases:

```sh
curl -LO https://github.com/duckdb/duckdb/releases/latest/download/duckdb_cli-linux-amd64.zip
unzip duckdb_cli-linux-amd64.zip
mkdir -p ~/.local/bin && mv duckdb ~/.local/bin/
```

Make sure `~/.local/bin` is on your `PATH`. If you'd rather use a distro package, check `apt search duckdb` or your distro's equivalent, but versions there may lag. Verify with:

```sh
duckdb --version
```

### First run

Replace `big.csv` with your file. Start with a preview:

```sh
duckdb -c "SELECT * FROM read_csv('big.csv') LIMIT 5"
```

Common tasks:

```sh
# Filter rows and pick columns, printed as CSV
duckdb -csv -c "SELECT id, name, amount
  FROM read_csv('big.csv') WHERE status = 'active'" > out.csv

# Group-by counts, most frequent first
duckdb -c "SELECT country, count(*) AS n
  FROM read_csv('big.csv') GROUP BY country ORDER BY n DESC"

# Write a filtered subset to a new file
duckdb -c "COPY (SELECT * FROM read_csv('big.csv') WHERE amount > 100)
  TO 'subset.csv' (HEADER)"
```

### Tips for multi-GB files

- **Type inference:** if a query fails partway through with a type error, the sampled types were wrong. Use `read_csv('big.csv', sample_size=-1)` to scan the whole file for types, or `all_varchar=true` to read everything as text and cast explicitly.
- **Memory and temp space:** cap memory and point spill files at a disk with room. Run these at the start of a session, or put them in a `.duckdbrc`-style init file:
  ```sql
  SET memory_limit = '4GB';
  SET temp_directory = '/path/with/space';
  ```
- **Interactive use:** run `duckdb` with no arguments to get a REPL, and use `.mode box` or `.mode markdown` for readable output.

### Alternatives

- **qsv** (Rust, single binary from GitHub releases): if you prefer pipeline-style commands, it has `select`, `search`, and `frequency` subcommands, and it is also quote-aware. Use it if you want shell pipelines rather than SQL.
- **Miller (`mlr`)**: a single Go binary with quote-aware CSV and an awk-like DSL. Some verbs, such as `sort`, hold data in memory, so it's less suited to 5 GB files than DuckDB or qsv.

Sources:
- DuckDB CLI installation and releases: https://duckdb.org/docs/installation/
- DuckDB CSV import options (sample_size, all_varchar): https://duckdb.org/docs/data/csv/overview
- qsv: https://github.com/dathere/qsv
- Miller: https://github.com/johnkerl/miller

text:
I'd go with **Bruno**. If your team is fine working only in the CLI, **Hurl** is a strong alternative.

I haven't run anything on this machine. The versions and flags below come from a quick web search, so check them against the official docs before you pin anything.

## Bruno

Bruno is a free, open-source (MIT) desktop API client, similar to Postman. It covers everything you asked for:

- **Plain-text files in git:** each request is its own small text file (`.bru`) inside a normal folder. They diff cleanly in pull requests.
- **Offline, no account:** there's no cloud workspace and no sign-in. The app just reads the folder.
- **Same files in CI:** the CLI (`@usebruno/cli`, command `bru`) runs the same folder on Linux. It exits with a non-zero code when an assertion fails, which fails the build. It can also write JUnit XML for your CI's test report.
- **Paid tier:** there's a paid "Golden Edition" with extra features, but you don't need it for this.

Assumption: Bruno's v3 release (planned for January 2026) adds YAML as a second file format. Either format works in git. Pick one for the whole team.

### Install (Mac)
```bash
brew install bruno            # desktop app
npm install -g @usebruno/cli  # CLI (needs Node.js); gives you `bru`
```

### First run
1. Open Bruno and choose **Create Collection**. Point it at a folder inside your repo, e.g. `api-tests/`.
2. Add an environment, such as `local`. It's saved as `api-tests/environments/local.bru` and holds variables like `baseUrl`. Mark tokens as **secret**: secret values stay on your machine and never go into git.
3. Create a request and add assertions. The saved file looks roughly like this:
   ```
   meta {
     name: Get user
     type: http
     seq: 1
   }

   get {
     url: {{baseUrl}}/users/1
   }

   assert {
     res.status: eq 200
     res.body.id: eq 1
   }

   tests {
     test("has email", function() {
       expect(res.body.email).to.be.a("string");
     });
   }
   ```
4. Run it from the terminal:
   ```bash
   cd api-tests
   bru run --env local
   ```
5. Commit the folder.

### CI (GitHub Actions example)
```yaml
- uses: actions/setup-node@v4
  with: { node-version: 20 }
- run: npm install -g @usebruno/cli@<pinned-version>
- run: bru run --env ci --env-var token=${{ secrets.API_TOKEN }} --reporter-junit results.xml
  working-directory: api-tests
```
If any assertion fails, `bru` exits non-zero and the job fails. Pin the CLI version so local and CI runs match. Guides disagree on the reporter flag (`--reporter-junit` vs. the older `--output … --format junit`), so run `bru run --help` for your version to check.

## Alternative: Hurl

Choose [Hurl](https://hurl.dev) if you don't need a GUI. It's open source, made by Orange, written in Rust, and the latest version I found is 8.0.x. Requests and assertions go in very small `.hurl` text files:
```
GET {{baseUrl}}/users/1
HTTP 200
[Asserts]
jsonpath "$.id" == 1
```
- **Install:** `brew install hurl` on Mac. In CI, use the Linux binary from GitHub releases or the Docker image `ghcr.io/orange-opensource/hurl`. Don't confuse it with an unrelated OCaml package also called "hurl".
- **Run:** `hurl --test --variable baseUrl=http://localhost:8080 api-tests/*.hurl --report-junit results.xml`. It's a single binary with no Node needed, and it exits non-zero when a test fails.
- **Downside:** there's no desktop app, so anyone used to Postman has to learn to work in text files.

**Rule of thumb:** pick Bruno if people want a Postman-like app. Pick Hurl if everyone is comfortable working only in the CLI and you want the smallest files and fastest CI runs.

Sources:
- [Bruno blog – 2025 recap / v3 plans](https://blog.usebruno.com/bruno-2025-from-idea-to-daily-driver)
- [Bruno CLI vs Apidog CLI](https://apidog.com/blog/bruno-cli-vs-apidog-cli/)
- [Bruno API testing guide](https://qaskills.sh/blog/bruno-api-testing-complete-guide)
- [Bruno API client overview](https://yrkan.com/blog/bruno-api-client/)
- [Hurl installation docs](https://hurl.dev/docs/installation.html)
- [Hurl 8.0.0 release](https://newreleases.io/project/github/Orange-OpenSource/hurl/release/8.0.0)

## 推薦：Backlog.md（`backlog` CLI）

我認為 **Backlog.md** 最符合你的需求。說明一下：[source] 的已驗證工具庫裡沒有這類工具，它回傳的結果都對不上。下面的資訊來自 Backlog.md 的官方 README，[source] 沒有幫它做沙箱測試。我也只是提供建議，沒有在你的機器上執行任何指令。

**為什麼選它：**
- **純文字、放在 repo 裡**：每個任務是一個 Markdown 檔，預設放在 `backlog/` 目錄，直接跟 git 一起 commit、diff、merge。
- **人和 agent 都能用**：CLI 可以新增、列出、編輯和封存任務。官方也提供 MCP server，Claude Code 和 Codex 都有現成的接法。
- **能輸出 JSON**：`task list`、`task view`、`search` 等指令都支援 `--json`。
- **符合你的條件**：MIT 授權、免費開源，README 寫明「no server, no account, no telemetry」，可離線使用，Mac 和 Linux 都能跑。

### 安裝（三選一）
```bash
brew install backlog-md      # macOS / Linux 有 Homebrew 時
npm i -g backlog.md          # 有 Node.js 時
bun i -g backlog.md          # 有 Bun 時
```

### 第一次使用
```bash
cd your-repo
backlog init "My Project"    # 精靈會問要不要接 AI（可選 MCP、CLI + 指示檔，或略過）

backlog task create "修正登入逾時問題"
backlog task list                    # 給人看
backlog task list --json             # 給 agent 讀
backlog task list -s "To Do" --json  # 依狀態篩選
backlog task edit 1 -s "Done"        # 關閉任務
backlog task archive 1               # 封存（要還原用 backlog task restore）

git add backlog && git commit -m "Add tasks"
```
註：README 沒有直接列出 `edit -s "Done"` 和 `archive 1` 的完整寫法，這兩行是我依照 CLI 的慣例推測的。執行前請先用 `backlog task edit --help` 確認。

### 接上 agent（選用，建議用 MCP）
```bash
claude mcp add backlog --scope user -- backlog mcp start
codex mcp add backlog backlog mcp start
```
`backlog init` 會自動把使用說明寫進 `CLAUDE.md` 和 `AGENTS.md`，兩個 agent 都會知道怎麼操作任務。如果你不想用 MCP，也可以叫 agent 直接下 `backlog task list --json` 這類指令。

## 其他選項
- **Beads（`bd`）**：專門為 coding agent 設計，每個指令都支援 `--json`，還有 `bd ready --json` 可以列出目前能做的任務。不過最新版改用 Dolt 資料庫儲存，舊版才是把 JSONL 存在 `.beads/`。所以「純文字、跟 git 一起管」這點不如 Backlog.md 單純。如果你想試，請先確認你裝的是哪個版本的儲存方式。安裝方式：`brew tap steveyegge/beads && brew install bd`，或 `npm install -g @beads/bd`，再到專案裡執行 `bd init`。
- **todo.txt CLI**：最簡單、純文字，但沒有內建 JSON 輸出，也沒有幫 agent 準備的整合，不太適合你的用法。

Sources:
- [MrLesk/Backlog.md (GitHub)](https://github.com/MrLesk/Backlog.md)
- [Backlog.md on SourcePulse](https://www.sourcepulse.org/projects/11036095)
- [steveyegge/beads (GitHub)](https://github.com/steveyegge/beads)

question: q04
text:
## Recommendation: SOPS + age

Use [SOPS](https://github.com/getsops/sops) to encrypt the `.env` files and [age](https://github.com/FiloSottile/age) for the keys. Both are free, open source, and run as local CLIs with no server. Each developer has their own age key pair. The committed `.sops.yaml` lists every member's **public** key as a recipient, so each person can decrypt with their own private key. Removing someone means removing their public key from that list and re-encrypting.

I'm assuming your secrets are plain `KEY=value` dotenv files and that everyone can use the terminal. I haven't run anything here, so check the current SOPS and age docs for exact flags.

## Install

**macOS**
```sh
brew install sops age
```

**Linux**
- `age`: use your package manager if it's packaged (for example `sudo apt install age`), or download a release binary from the age GitHub releases page.
- `sops`: download the binary or `.deb`/`.rpm` from the SOPS GitHub releases page.

Verify with `sops --version` and `age --version`.

## First-run setup (once, by the person who sets up the repo)

1. **Create your key:**
   ```sh
   mkdir -p ~/.config/sops/age
   age-keygen -o ~/.config/sops/age/keys.txt
   ```
   The output prints a public key starting with `age1...`. On macOS, SOPS also looks in `~/Library/Application Support/sops/age/keys.txt`. Setting `SOPS_AGE_KEY_FILE` to your key path works on both platforms.

2. **Create `.sops.yaml` at the repo root**, with one public key per teammate:
   ```yaml
   creation_rules:
     - path_regex: \.env(\..+)?$
       age: >-
         age1alice...,
         age1bob...,
         age1carol...,
         age1dan...
   ```

3. **Encrypt the existing file and remove the plaintext:**
   ```sh
   sops --encrypt --input-type dotenv --output-type dotenv --in-place .env
   ```
   Commit the encrypted file. Add plaintext `.env` files to `.gitignore` so they can't be committed by accident.

4. **Add a guard against plaintext leaks:** a pre-commit hook such as gitleaks is a good option.

## Daily use

- **Edit secrets:** `sops .env` opens the decrypted file in your editor and re-encrypts on save.
- **Run an app:** `sops exec-env .env 'npm run dev'`. This injects the variables without writing a plaintext file to disk.
- **Decrypt to a file (only if a tool requires one):** `sops decrypt .env > .env.local`, then make sure `.env.local` is in `.gitignore`.

## Onboarding a new developer

1. They run `age-keygen` and send you their **public** key. Public keys are safe to share in chat or a PR.
2. Add the key to `.sops.yaml`.
3. Run `sops updatekeys .env` for each encrypted file. This needs a current member's private key.
4. Commit and push. The new person can now decrypt.

Never share a private key (the `AGE-SECRET-KEY-...` line).

## Offboarding (the part you care most about)

1. Remove their public key from `.sops.yaml`.
2. Run `sops updatekeys` on every encrypted file.
3. Commit and push.
4. **Rotate every secret they could read.** This step matters most. They already have decrypted values, and old commits still contain ciphertext they can decrypt with their key. Removing the key stops future access, but it doesn't undo past access. Rotation is the only real cut-off.

## Other points to plan for

- **CI:** create a dedicated age key for CI, add its public key to `.sops.yaml`, and store the private key as a CI secret.
- **Key backup:** each person should keep a backup of their private key in a password manager. If someone loses their key, they need to be re-added the same way as onboarding.
- **Team size:** with 4 people, the manual `updatekeys` step takes seconds, so no extra tooling is needed.

## Alternatives I'd rule out

- **git-crypt:** it works, but it's built around GPG keyrings, and removing a member cleanly is harder.
- **dotenvx:** it's free and open source, but teams usually share one project private key, which defeats per-person revocation.
- **Hosted tools (Doppler, Infisical Cloud, 1Password, etc.):** you excluded these.

Sources: no web sources used. This is based on my knowledge of the SOPS and age projects, and I didn't verify current versions or flags.

I checked [source], which keeps a catalog of tools it has actually installed and tested. None of the 18 tools it has verified fits this request. It did name Hurl as a likely fit but hasn't tested it. Everything below comes from my own knowledge, not a test run, so check the details against the official docs. As you asked, I didn't run any commands on your machine.

**My assumption:** you're moving off Postman or something like it, and your team wants a desktop app on Mac plus a CLI in CI. If your team is happy working only in the terminal, see option 2.

## Main recommendation: Bruno (MIT-licensed, offline, no account)

- **Git-friendly files:** each request is one plain-text file (`.bru`) inside a normal folder. You commit the folder to your repo, and each changed request shows up as a small, readable diff. Newer versions also offer a YAML-based format.
- **Works offline:** the desktop app has no cloud workspace and needs no sign-in.
- **CI:** the `bru` CLI runs the same files on Linux. If any assertion fails, it exits with a non-zero code, so the build fails. It can also write JUnit reports.
- **Cost:** the core app and CLI are free and open source. There's an optional paid "Golden Edition", but you don't need it for this.

### Install (Mac)
```bash
brew install --cask bruno          # desktop app
npm install -g @usebruno/cli       # CLI (needs Node 18+), command is `bru`
```

### First run
1. Open Bruno, click **Create Collection**, and pick a folder inside your repo, e.g. `api-tests/`.
2. Add a request. Bruno saves it as a file like this:
   ```
   meta { name: Get user  type: http  seq: 1 }

   get {
     url: {{baseUrl}}/users/1
   }

   assert {
     res.status: eq 200
     res.body.id: eq 1
   }

   tests {
     test("has email", function() {
       expect(res.getBody().email).to.be.a("string");
     });
   }
   ```
3. Create an environment (stored as `environments/ci.bru`) that sets `baseUrl`. Keep secrets out of git: reference them as `{{process.env.API_TOKEN}}` and put the real values in a `.env` file listed in `.gitignore`.
4. Run it locally the same way CI will:
   ```bash
   cd api-tests
   bru run --env ci
   ```
5. CI step, shown for GitHub Actions (other CI systems work the same way):
   ```yaml
   - run: npm install -g @usebruno/cli
   - run: bru run --env ci --reporter-junit results.xml
     working-directory: api-tests
     env:
       API_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.API_TOKEN }}
   ```
   The reporter flag has changed between CLI versions (older versions used `--output results.xml --format junit`). Run `bru run --help` on the version you install to confirm. Also pin the CLI version in CI so local and CI runs behave the same.

## Option 2: Hurl (Apache-2.0, CLI only)
Hurl suits you if you don't need a desktop app. Each `.hurl` file is a plain-text list of requests with assertions written underneath. It's a single fast binary written in Rust (no Node needed), and its files diff very cleanly.
```bash
brew install hurl
hurl --test --report-junit results.xml tests/*.hurl
```
Example file:
```
GET {{base_url}}/users/1
HTTP 200
[Asserts]
jsonpath "$.id" == 1
```
On Linux CI, use the `.deb` package, the release tarball or the Docker image `ghcr.io/orange-opensource/hurl`.

## Other options
- **httpYac:** runs standard `.http` / `.rest` files. It has a VS Code extension and a CLI (`httpyac send --all`) that works in CI. It's a good fit if your team already writes `.http` files.

**Bottom line:** choose Bruno if people want a Postman-style app. Choose Hurl if everyone is comfortable in the terminal and you want the simplest CI setup.

text:
**Recommendation: don't install a proxy. Ollama already serves an OpenAI-compatible API at `http://localhost:11434/v1`.** Point the official `openai` client at it, and your script can often run unchanged.

I'm assuming Ollama is already installed and working, and that the script uses the `openai` v1 Python client (`from openai import OpenAI`). If you're on an older Ollama build, update it first.

## Setup

1. **Confirm Ollama is installed and running.** On Ubuntu the install script sets up a systemd service:
   ```bash
   curl -fsSL https://ollama.com/install.sh | sh
   systemctl status ollama
   ```
   If the service isn't running, start it with `sudo systemctl start ollama`, or run `ollama serve` in a separate terminal.

2. **Pull a model.** Use whichever fits your hardware:
   ```bash
   ollama pull llama3.2        # small, runs on most machines
   ollama pull qwen2.5-coder   # better for code
   ```

3. **Smoke-test the endpoint:**
   ```bash
   curl http://localhost:11434/v1/models
   ```
   You should see your pulled models listed.

## Point the script at Ollama

Option A: no code changes, using environment variables. The v1 `openai` client reads these by default:
```bash
export OPENAI_BASE_URL=http://localhost:11434/v1
export OPENAI_API_KEY=ollama   # required by the client, ignored by Ollama
python your_script.py
```

Option B: change the client in code:
```python
from openai import OpenAI

client = OpenAI(
    base_url="http://localhost:11434/v1",
    api_key="ollama",  # any non-empty string
)

resp = client.chat.completions.create(
    model="llama3.2",  # must be an Ollama model name, not "gpt-4o"
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Hello"}],
)
print(resp.choices[0].message.content)
```

**Things to check in your script:**
- **Model names.** Anything like `gpt-4o` or `gpt-4.1` must become a model you've pulled, such as `llama3.2`. If you don't want to edit every call, add a `model=` mapping at the top of the script.
- **Unsupported features.** Ollama covers chat completions, streaming, embeddings, and most tool calling and JSON mode, depending on the model. It does not support OpenAI-only APIs such as Assistants, Files, Batch, or fine-tuning. Check the Ollama OpenAI compatibility docs if your script uses one of those.

## When you'd want a gateway instead

Install **LiteLLM Proxy** only if you need something Ollama doesn't provide, such as one endpoint that routes to several backends (Ollama plus a cloud model), per-key limits, or logging:
```bash
python3 -m venv ~/litellm && source ~/litellm/bin/activate
pip install 'litellm[proxy]'
litellm --model ollama/llama3.2 --port 4000
```
Then set `base_url="http://localhost:4000"`. Start with the direct Ollama approach, since it has fewer moving parts.

Sources (from memory, not checked against live pages this session):
- Ollama OpenAI compatibility: https://github.com/ollama/ollama/blob/main/docs/openai.md
- LiteLLM proxy quickstart: https://docs.litellm.ai/docs/proxy/quick_start

text:
# Use qsv

Install **qsv** ([github.com/dathere/qsv](https://github.com/dathere/qsv)). It is the maintained successor to BurntSushi's `xsv`, written in Rust, and released under MIT/Unlicense. It ships as one static binary with no runtime. Its CSV parser follows RFC 4180, so quoted fields that contain commas and line breaks are handled correctly. It streams the file instead of loading it into memory, and once you build an index it uses all your cores. A 2–5 GB file should be no problem.

My assumptions: x86_64 Linux, and UTF-8 CSV with standard double-quote escaping. I didn't run anything on this machine.

## Install

1. Open the [releases page](https://github.com/dathere/qsv/releases/latest) and download the asset named `qsv-<version>-x86_64-unknown-linux-musl.zip`. The musl build is fully static, so it runs on any distro. Use the `aarch64` build on ARM.
2. Unzip it and install it:
   ```bash
   unzip qsv-*-x86_64-unknown-linux-musl.zip -d qsv-dl
   install -m 755 qsv-dl/qsv ~/.local/bin/    # or sudo install ... /usr/local/bin/
   qsv --version
   ```
   The zip also contains `qsvlite` and `qsvdp`, which are smaller variants. You only need `qsv`.

qsv is in Homebrew, Nix, Arch (AUR) and Scoop, but it generally isn't in the Debian, Ubuntu or Fedora repos. If you need a distro package, see Miller below.

## First run

```bash
qsv index big.csv                 # one-time; writes big.csv.idx, makes count/frequency/stats fast + parallel
qsv headers big.csv               # list column names with their positions
qsv count big.csv                 # row count (instant once indexed)

# Pick columns
qsv select id,status,country big.csv > slim.csv

# Filter rows (regex on one column), then pick columns
qsv search -s status '^shipped$' big.csv | qsv select id,country,amount > shipped.csv

# Group-by count on one column (all values, sorted by count)
qsv frequency -s country --limit 0 big.csv

# Multi-column group-by, or filter+group in one step (SQL via the built-in Polars engine)
qsv sqlp big.csv "SELECT country, status, COUNT(*) AS n
                  FROM _t_1 WHERE amount > 100
                  GROUP BY country, status ORDER BY n DESC"
```

A few other commands that help: `qsv stats big.csv` profiles each column, `qsv slice -l 20 big.csv | qsv table` gives a quick look at the data, and `qsv sort` and `qsv dedup` do what their names say. `qsv --list` shows every command.

## Alternatives

- **DuckDB CLI** (MIT license, single binary, `duckdb_cli-linux-amd64.zip` on its GitHub releases page). Pick this if most of your work is SQL-style grouping, joins or aggregations. It's very fast, multithreaded, and runs out-of-core:
  ```bash
  duckdb -c "SELECT country, status, count(*) n FROM read_csv('big.csv') GROUP BY ALL ORDER BY n DESC"
  ```
- **Miller (`mlr`)** (BSD license, single Go binary). Pick this if you must install from your distro's repos: `apt install miller` or `dnf install miller`. It's slower than qsv or DuckDB on files this big, but it parses CSV correctly and its syntax is friendly:
  ```bash
  mlr --icsv --opprint filter '$amount > 100' then count -g country,status big.csv
  ```
- **Avoid plain `xsv`.** It works, but it's no longer maintained, and qsv covers everything it does.

In short: use qsv for everyday filter, select and count work, and add DuckDB when the queries get complex.

**My recommendation is to install nothing extra.** Ollama already serves an **OpenAI-compatible API** at `http://localhost:11434/v1`. It supports chat completions, completions, embeddings and model listing. The official `openai` Python package (v1.x) reads `OPENAI_BASE_URL` and `OPENAI_API_KEY` from the environment, so you may not even need to edit the script.

I'm assuming the script uses `openai` v1 or later (`from openai import OpenAI`) and calls chat completions.

## Steps

1. **Check that Ollama is running and has a model:**
   ```bash
   ollama list                      # see installed models
   ollama pull llama3.1             # if you need one
   curl http://localhost:11434/v1/models
   ```

2. **Point the script at Ollama with environment variables:**
   ```bash
   export OPENAI_BASE_URL=http://localhost:11434/v1
   export OPENAI_API_KEY=ollama     # needed by the client, but Ollama ignores it
   python your_script.py
   ```
   You can also set it in code:
   ```python
   client = OpenAI(base_url="http://localhost:11434/v1", api_key="ollama")
   ```

3. **Fix the model name.** If the script asks for a fixed name like `"gpt-4o"`, Ollama will return "model not found." You can either change the name in the script to a local model (e.g. `"llama3.1"`), or make a copy of the local model under the OpenAI name so the script works unchanged:
   ```bash
   ollama cp llama3.1 gpt-4o
   ```

4. **Test it quickly:**
   ```bash
   curl http://localhost:11434/v1/chat/completions \
     -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
     -d '{"model":"gpt-4o","messages":[{"role":"user","content":"Say hi"}]}'
   ```

**Limits:** Plain chat, streaming, JSON mode, embeddings and (with models that support it) tool calling work well. Newer endpoints are less certain. If your script uses the Assistants API, the Responses API (`client.responses.create`), audio or image generation, check Ollama's OpenAI-compatibility docs for your version. Some of these may not be supported.

## If you do want a gateway: LiteLLM Proxy

A gateway is worth adding if you want name mapping, fallback to the real OpenAI, several backends, API keys or request logging. LiteLLM is the standard choice for that.

```bash
python3 -m venv ~/litellm && source ~/litellm/bin/activate
pip install 'litellm[proxy]'
```

`config.yaml`:
```yaml
model_list:
  - model_name: gpt-4o              # name your script asks for
    litellm_params:
      model: ollama_chat/llama3.1   # local Ollama model
      api_base: http://localhost:11434
```

Run it and point the script at it:
```bash
litellm --config config.yaml        # listens on port 4000 by default
export OPENAI_BASE_URL=http://localhost:4000
export OPENAI_API_KEY=anything      # or a master_key if you configure one
python your_script.py
```

**In short:** start with Ollama's built-in `/v1` endpoint and two environment variables. Add LiteLLM only if you need features Ollama doesn't provide.

I haven't run anything or changed any files. This is based on the projects' docs.

## Recommendation: use ollmcp (MCP Client for Ollama)

[ollmcp](https://github.com/jonigl/mcp-client-for-ollama/wiki) fits what you described:
- It's a free, open-source (MIT) terminal chat app for local Ollama models.
- It starts stdio MCP servers as subprocesses. Stdio is its default transport.
- It needs no account. It talks to your local Ollama at `http://localhost:11434`.
- It can reload your servers without restarting (`rs`), which is useful while you work on your own server.

### Install
```bash
# Requires Python 3.10+ and Ollama already installed
uv tool install --upgrade ollmcp      # or: pipx install ollmcp / pip install --upgrade ollmcp
```

### First run
1. **Pull a model that supports tool calling.** Models without tool support will chat but never call your tools.
   ```bash
   ollama pull qwen2.5:7b      # or qwen3, llama3.1:8b, mistral-nemo, etc.
   ```
   Make sure Ollama is running: `systemctl status ollama` or `ollama serve`.

2. **Add your stdio servers.** The command to launch each server goes after `--`.
   ```bash
   # Filesystem server, limited to the directories you list
   ollmcp mcp add filesystem -- npx -y @modelcontextprotocol/server-filesystem ~/projects ~/notes

   # Your own server (adjust the command to how you launch it)
   ollmcp mcp add ourtool --env API_MODE=local -- python3 /path/to/our_server.py
   # or: ollmcp mcp add ourtool -- uv run --directory /path/to/ourtool server.py

   ollmcp mcp list
   ```

3. **Start chatting.**
   ```bash
   ollmcp --model qwen2.5:7b
   ```
   It connects to the saved servers on its own. Use the in-app help to switch tools on or off, change models, or reload servers (`rs`) after you edit your server code.

Flags and subcommands have changed between versions, so check `ollmcp --help` and `ollmcp mcp --help` for the version you install.

## Keeping everything on your machine
- **Avoid Ollama cloud models.** Models with a `:cloud` tag, or anything reached through ollama.com sign-in, run remotely. Use only models you've pulled locally.
- **Downloads are separate from your chats.** Installing ollmcp, pulling models and the first `npx -y` fetch of the filesystem server all download from the internet. None of that sends your conversations anywhere. To be fully offline afterward, install the filesystem server once (`npm i -g @modelcontextprotocol/server-filesystem`) and point the command at it instead of using `npx -y`.
- **Leave the other providers off.** ollmcp can also talk to OpenAI-compatible endpoints. As long as you only use Ollama on localhost, nothing goes out.
- **Limit what the model can touch.** Give the filesystem server only the directories you want the model to read or write. Keep ollmcp's tool confirmation on so you approve each tool call.

## Alternatives
- **[MCPHost](https://github.com/mark3labs/mcphost)** is a Go CLI. Install it with `go install github.com/mark3labs/mcphost@latest`. You list servers in `~/.mcphost.json` or `.yml`, then run `mcphost -m ollama:qwen2.5:7b`. It's a good choice if you'd rather have a single binary and a config file, or want to use it in scripts. Its config format has changed between versions (newer ones use `"type": "local"` for stdio), so check the README ([ClickHouse guide](https://clickhouse.com/docs/guides/use-cases/ai-ml/MCP/ollama) has an example).
- **oterm** is a full-screen terminal chat app built for Ollama, and it also supports MCP servers. It's worth a look if you mainly want a nicer chat window.

Sources:
- [mcp-client-for-ollama wiki](https://github.com/jonigl/mcp-client-for-ollama/wiki)
- [ollmcp on PyPI](https://pypi.org/project/mcp-client-for-ollama/0.35.1/)
- [mcp.so listing](https://mcp.so/servers/mcp-client-for-ollama)
- [ClickHouse: MCP with Ollama (MCPHost)](https://clickhouse.com/docs/guides/use-cases/ai-ml/MCP/ollama)
- [MCPHost PR/README](https://github.com/mark3labs/mcphost/pull/44/files)
- [localaimaster Ollama MCP guide](https://localaimaster.com/blog/ollama-mcp-integration)
